Chapter 6 Figure 6-4. Climbing helmets 6-46. The issued MOLLE pack is not suited for rock climbing. Its size, empty weight, and width interfere with movements necessary for even moderate climbing. When loaded, climbing may not even be possible. Soldiers climbing sustained rock routes may require a smaller lightweight pack to carry required items (for example, water, sensitive items, communications equipment) during the climb. Whatever packs are worn should be snugged to the body, and waist straps as well as chest straps worn to reduce the load from shifting during climbing and throwing the climber out of balance. ROCK CLIMBING DURING MILITARY OPERATIONS 6-47. Sustained climbing in 5th-class terrain during conventional military operations is impractical. However, routes through easier terrain are often blocked by shorter sections of 4th or easier 5th-class terrain. These routes may be the only or most tactically sound approaches to points of domination for properly trained units. Small teams of advanced military mountaineers can be used to establish fixed-rope routes for lesser-trained Soldiers to use for protection during movement. Accessing these points may be required to reach enemy defensive positions, establish observation posts, or position small teams conducting reconnaissance or forward observation of fires. 6-48. Soldiers climbing 4th- and 5th-class terrain are typically unable to provide themselves sufficient local security during movement. Bounding overwatch in vertical terrain by small-specialized teams or VDA-crossing procedures must be performed by a larger unit to provide adequate security for climbing Soldiers. (See ATP 3-21.50 for more on VDA.) Small reconnaissance and surveillance teams may have to rely on careful technical route selection that provides concealment throughout the approach and the climb. Fortunately, 4th-class and easier 5th-class terrain often provide such opportunities for teams with the technical and mobility skills necessary to negotiate them. CLIMBING ROUTE SELECTION 6-49. Before climbing, Soldiers should scan the rock for features that indicate that climbing the route is possible. With experience, Soldiers can determine how difficult a section of rock will be for them to complete. 92 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

(See chapter 10 on how to protect climbers from fall hazards.) 6-50. During military operations, the least difficult routes possible should be selected for travel. (See chapter 7 for more information on planning technical movement routes.) ROCK-CLIMBING TECHNIQUES 6-51. The basic principles for rock climbing are the same as those for walking in rough terrain. They are finding and selecting suitable holds and positioning the body to achieve sufficient friction for continued movement. Due to the vertical nature of the terrain, hands must be used to aid Soldiers in maintaining balance and preventing them from tipping backward off the rock. 6-52. Suspect rock-climbing holds should be tested to ensure they are secure by tapping with a hand or foot. Holds that move or shift should be avoided. This is common in undeveloped 4th- and 5th-class terrain. Maintaining Balance 6-53. Balance is the most important aspect of rock climbing and footwork is the foundation of balance. Good use of the feet saves energy and makes staying in balance easier. A relaxed, comfortable

undeveloped 4th- and 5th-class terrain. Maintaining Balance 6-53. Balance is the most important aspect of rock climbing and footwork is the foundation of balance. Good use of the feet saves energy and makes staying in balance easier. A relaxed, comfortable stance is essential. The body should be centered over the feet as much as possible. On lower angle sections of climbing, it should be positioned away from the rock face. Alternatively, it should be positioned closer to the rock face on steeper sections. This puts downward pressure on footholds, increasing their security. Smaller lower body movements are often less strenuous than larger ones, which take more effort to stay in balance. 6-54. Rock climbing usually requires the use of handholds to maintain balance. Handholds can be large jugs that allow climbers to hold nearly their whole weight or tiny crimpers that only hold a fraction of their weight. Specific handhold techniques are discussed throughout this section. New climbers commonly overuse their arms to pull themselves up the rock and burn out quickly. Tired or pumped forearms are a sign of bad footwork. 6-55. Whenever possible, three points of contact should be maintained while moving the fourth to the next hold.

their arms to pull themselves up the rock and burn out quickly. Tired or pumped forearms are a sign of bad footwork. 6-55. Whenever possible, three points of contact should be maintained while moving the fourth to the next hold. This can reduce the likelihood of a fall should one point of contact fail. Types of Contact 6-56. Though counterintuitive, often pushing rather than pulling is required during climbing. Using downward pressure involves pushing down on a feature with the hands to allow unweighting of the other hand or one foot for movement to the next hold. Using counterpressure involves pushing away from features to allow a hand or foot to be unweighted for movement. (See figure 6-5, page 94.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 93

Chapter 6 Figure 6-5. Downward or counterpressure 6-57. Occasionally, the holds available put the climber out of balance, but repositioning the body (usually by extending a leg to the left or right) improves the climber’s balance. This technique is called counterbalancing and often allows the climber greater reach. (See figure 6-6.) Often the climber can find a microfeature to touch or apply slight pressure to with the foot improving the security of the move. 94 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-6. Counterbalance 6-58. Occasionally, the climber must switch hands or feet on a hold to make the next move. Sometimes the hold can be shared temporarily by two hands or feet, even if they are unsecure, while the lead hand or lead foot moves. Other times, the second hand or foot may need to use a temporary, perhaps less desirable hold, while the lead one moves. 6-59. Dynamic moves are sudden, explosive moves where climbers throw themselves out of balance, potentially even losing contact with the rock, to reach another hold. These moves must be calculated carefully because failing to execute them perfectly usually results in a fall. Slab and Face Climbing 6-60. Slabs are typically smoother, lower angle rock features. They can be large or small. Comparatively, they provide the climber with few hands and footholds and require good footwork and balancing to climb. The primary technique used to climb them is smearing with the feet. This involves placing the sole of the boot or shoe on the rock with toe facing uphill to obtain maximum contact and friction. The body is then positioned away from the rock so that the foot does not slip. The

This involves placing the sole of the boot or shoe on the rock with toe facing uphill to obtain maximum contact and friction. The body is then positioned away from the rock so that the foot does not slip. The closer climbers can get to pushing perpendicular to the rock, the more friction they will create. (See figure 6-7, page 96.) Hands are usually used to help balance by pushing against the rock. Any microfeature that can be found will improve the security of climbing slabby terrain. Climbing slabby rock helps build confidence in footwork and good balance skills. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 95

Chapter 6 6-61. Face climbing is what is commonly associated with rock climbing. Face climbs are typically suitably featured rock faces (cliffs) where climbers employ a wide variety of basic moves to ascending. Climbers spend most of their time facing the rock, like climbing a ladder. Many footholds are small or sloped and require edging or smearing to be effective; others are larger. (See figure 6-8.) Many techniques for using handholds exist. (See figure 6-8.) Using knees should be avoided because they are more likely to slip than good footwear. 6-62. Most slab or face climbing terrain appropriate to military operations can be climbed in combat boots, mountaineering boots, or approach shoes. Moderate to difficult climbs require climbing shoes. (See figure 6-9.) Figure 6-7. Footholds Figure 6-8. Handhold techniques 96 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-9. Slab body position Resting During Climbing 6-63. Resting is critical during sustained rock climbing. Any opportunity to stand up and let go or lightly hold on with the hands should be taken. Sometimes the body or a body part can be wedged into a large crack, allowing the climber to relax. Often, the only rests available are between moves while looking for the next hold. When not actively moving, climbers should keep their weight on their skeletal system as much as possible. This means locking out legs or arms and providing muscles with a brief rest. Doing this is particularly important to preserve arm strength. Often one arm and the climbers’ feet can support their weight while they shake out the other arm and hand. (See figure 6-10, page 98.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 97

Chapter 6 Figure 6-10. Rest or shake out Specific Moves 6-64. Mantling involves pulling down with both arms on the edge of a ledge type feature until the chest is ledge height, then transitioning to pushing down on the ledge while walking the feet up the face below. This move is common to climbing out of a swimming pool. (See figure 6-11.) 98 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility 6-65. Stemming involves placing the feet on features to the left and right of the body so that force is applied outward as well as down. Stemming is typically very stable and requires a relatively low amount of energy to maintain. (See figure 6-12, page 100.) 6-66. Underclinging involves gripping an overhanging rock feature with the hands, palm up, and pushing against a lower rock face with the feet. Underclings can be very stable but can be quite strenuous and tiring. Occasionally, underlings are the only means of getting through a section of climbing. (See figure 6-13, page 101.) 6-67. Liebacking involves using counterforce by pulling hard on a vertical or diagonal feature (such as a large flake) while pushing hard against the face of the rock. These moves are very strenuous because little or none of the climbers’ weights is supported by their feet. In fact, leg muscles are being used to push away from the rock, so they are very taxing to the upper body. The climber’s hands are then walked up the feature while the feet are walked up the face. Footholds on the face, however small, can be used to make liebacking easier and

Footholds on the face, however small, can be used to make liebacking easier and more secure. (See figure 6-14, page 102.) Figure 6-11. Mantling 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 99

Chapter 6 Figure 6-14. Liebacking Crack Climbing 6-68. Crack climbing requires a specific set of nonintuitive techniques that take quite a bit of practice to build proficiency in. While some climbs involving cracks can be climbed with weak or no crack technique, more difficult crack climbs require climbing shoes and good technique to be climbable. Mixed crack climbing involves using features on the rock face for footholds while using a prominent crack for handholds. (See figure 6-15.) Classic crack climbing involves moving up a prominent crack by alternately jamming hands or fingers and feet or toes and walking them up the crack. Often, one foot is placed out of the crack to the side for balance, even on a featureless face. Off-width crack climbing is the term for climbing cracks that are larger than fist and foot sized but not large enough to fit the entire body. These climbs are difficult. 102 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-15. Mixed face and crack climbing Jamming 6-69. A critical technique in climbing cracks involves placing a hand or foot into a crack and turning, twisting, or otherwise manipulating them so that they become temporarily jammed in the crack. A good jam can be achieved in a variety of ways depending on crack size, whether it has constrictions in it or not, and its position in relation to other holds on the climb. Jams can provide solid hands or footholds but are often uncomfortable or even painful. Crack size determines which jam technique to use for a given hold. Constrictions in the crack make jam holds more secure. Types of Hand Jams 6-70. Hand-sized jams are the easiest to perform. The hand is inserted open into the crack and then the fingers bent exert pressure against the walls of the crack. Often turning one hand thumb down is useful. Typically, leaning to the same side adds security to a thumb up hand jam. (See figure 6-16, page 104 for variations of hand jamming.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 103

Chapter 6 6-71. Fist jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are larger than those that work for hand jams. The same jamming principles apply, but climbers just insert their entire fist into the crack. (See figure 6-17 for variations of fist jamming.) 6-72. Finger jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are smaller than those that will accept a hand. The same jamming principles apply, but the climber only inserts their fingers, or parts of their fingers into the crack. Finger jamming is more difficult and can be painful for the joints. It is important to strengthen finger muscles prior to attempting to support substantial weight with finger jams to prevent joint strain. (See figure 6-18.) Types of Foot Jams 6-73. Foot jams involve turning the foot so that it fits into the crack and then twisting it so that the width of the foot wedges into the crack. This can be uncomfortable but can provide very secure footholds. (See figure 6-19.) 6-74. Toe jams are used in the same manner as foot jams, but in smaller cracks. (See figure 6-20, page 106.) Arm bars is a technique used for off-width cracks and involves inserting an entire arm into the crack and bending at the elbow to create a jam. (See figure 6-21, page 106.) 6-76. Chicken wing is a technique also used for off-width cracks and involves inserting an entire arm into the crack bent at the elbow and pushing against one wall of the crack with the hand to create a jam. Climbing dihedrals and chimneys involves positioning the body inside a feature and using counterpressure or stemming to make upward movement. These features can often make for less strenuous climbing due to the counterpressure positions allowing for more rests. A dihedral is two rock faces that meet to form a corner, like an open book. Often there is a crack where the two faces meet. Chimneys are roughly parallel-sided features. They could be like a vertical shaft or crack large enough to accept a whole body. 6-78. Dihedrals can usually be climbed with a combination of stemming and either crack or face climbing. Dihedrals are easier and less strenuous to climb when the two faces have multiple and large features. 6-79. Chimneys are often unpleasant features to climb but provide a lot of security during movement. The basic technique for climbers is to position their body in the chimney and use counterpressure by pushing with arms, legs, and back against opposing sides. (See figures 6-22 through 6-24, pages 107 through 109, for variations in chimney climbing techniques.) Often during chimney climbing, it is

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-24. Chimney climbing technique Traversing 6-80. Traversing is moving laterally on the rock. This is often necessary because the features that make up a rock route are not always continuous or travel straight up a face. Traversing often involves a series of placement exchanges. Most traversing is done facing the rock. 6-81. Hand traversing requires a ledge, flake, other horizontal feature, or a series of horizontally oriented large handholds. Climbers’ hands walk their way across the features while their feet walk their way across a face below. (See figure 6-25, page 110.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 109

Chapter 6 6-82. Steep traverse is a technique often used when handholds are not as good, but decent footholds are present. Climbers lean heavily in the direction they want to move and place hands on available holds, and then walk their feet in the same direction using available footholds. Sometimes a crossover step is helpful. This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and counterforce skills. (See figure 6-26.) Figure 6-25. Hand traverse Topping Out or Gaining Ledges 6-83. Topping out or gaining a ledge can be one of the more challenging parts of climbing. Often low holds located near where climbers want to put their feet need to be used to get over the edge. Often, a mantling technique is effective. Most importantly, climbers should avoid laying on their belly on the edge when moving because it may be difficult to get their feel back on the rock, and they may slide off on sloped ledges. A crossover step is helpful. This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and counterforce skills. (See figure 6-26 for the proper technique.) 110 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-26. Gaining ledges Down Climbing 6-84. Down climbing is far more difficult than climbing up and takes much practice to gain proficiency. This is largely because rock features are often difficult to identify from above. They are easily obscured by other features above them or even the climber’s body parts. However, down climbing is an important skill to practice, as it is often necessary to do in 3rd- and 4th-class terrain. 6-85. Facing out is a technique used on low angle rock. Climbers face out and use their hands for stability behind and below their body while moving their feet down to the next hold. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-86. Walking down a slab is a technique that involves simply walking down slabby rock while maintaining maximum friction and balance. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-87. Facing sideways involves climbers facing to the side and side stepping down to lower footholds while controlling and balancing their movement using handholds above. Climbers use this technique on steeper rock. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-88. Facing the rock involves climbing down in the same position as the climber would use to move up the rock. Climbers lower themselves

movement using handholds above. Climbers use this technique on steeper rock. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 6-88. Facing the rock involves climbing down in the same position as the climber would use to move up the rock. Climbers lower themselves down with their arms, keeping their body away from the rock so they can see footholds below, and then transition their weight onto the next foothold. (See figure 6-27, page 112.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 111

Chapter 6 Figure 6-27. Down climbing TRAINING FOR ROCK CLIMBING 6-89. Beginner rock-climbing training is typically conducted at established climbing areas using top rope belay techniques (see chapter 10). When supervised by qualified mountaineers, this kind of rock climbing is relatively low risk and has a high payoff for developing mobility skills. One restriction is that sites do not often allow large groups to be actively engaged. Thus, climbing training should be planned along with concurrent training for smaller groups to rotate through. Route difficulty should be challenging to climbers but easy enough that they can be successful. This motivates climbers to build skills. A motivational rather than critical atmosphere is most effective when building climbing skills. 6-90. Climbing training for more advanced military mountaineers can be conducted the same way, just on more challenging routes, but should also be conducted in a multipitch setting that more accurately reproduces conditions of climbing during military operations. This setting requires the development of lead climbing and route-finding skills, which are critical to the advanced military mountaineer. 6-91. Leaders should try to learn the etiquette associated with climbing before using civilian climbing areas. 112 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility SECTION II – MOVEMENT OVER SNOW AND ICE 6-92. Deep snow, steep powdery slopes, glare ice, and frozen waterfalls all present significant challenges to movement. The basic individual movement principles and skill development necessary for movement under other surface conditions also apply to movement over snow and ice. However, additional skills are necessary for efficiency and safety. Specialized equipment is required in even the easiest snow or ice-covered terrain. MOBILITY OVER SNOW AND ICE 6-93. Fitness and movement techniques are the foundation of moving through snow or up steep ice. However, identifying and selecting secure foot placements can be difficult because traction is drastically reduced. Movement without specialized equipment, such as crampons or skis, is difficult under almost all conditions above 1st-class terrain. Even when it is possible, deep snow requires a substantial amount of energy to move through unaided. Anything deeper than calf-deep snow will impede movement in even easy terrain, and a few inches of snow or a glaze of ice will make steeper terrain treacherous. Soldiers must develop the same level of skill using snow and ice equipment, which requires proficiency in an additional set of skills. Like moving over broken rocky terrain, these skills

or a glaze of ice will make steeper terrain treacherous. Soldiers must develop the same level of skill using snow and ice equipment, which requires proficiency in an additional set of skills. Like moving over broken rocky terrain, these skills can only be developed through experience and repetition. Units that train their Soldiers to proficiency in these conditions can move faster, safer, and access terrain that others cannot. EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE 6-94. Skis provide substantial floatation in deep snow and require the least amount of energy for movement. This is especially true for downhill movement where much energy can be saved over walking. There are varieties of ski systems available for movement over snow, but those most suited to military mountaineering are called alpine touring skis. The ski itself is like a downhill ski, but the binding allows the heel to release for movement over flat or uphill terrain. It can also be locked down for greater control when skiing downhill. Climbing skins are used in conjunction with skis to climb uphill. Skins are designed to slide in only one direction, providing traction in deep snow and on steep slopes. At a minimum, a stiff mountaineering boot is

when skiing downhill. Climbing skins are used in conjunction with skis to climb uphill. Skins are designed to slide in only one direction, providing traction in deep snow and on steep slopes. At a minimum, a stiff mountaineering boot is necessary for use with skis. In the steepest terrain, a dedicated rigid plastic ski boot may be required. Compatibility between boots and bindings must be considered. (See figure 6-28, page 114.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 113

Chapter 6 Figure 6-28. Alpine touring skis 6-95. Snowshoes are another tool available to Soldiers for moving over deep snow. Modern snowshoes provide sufficient floatation and traction for moving through snow on fairly steep (class 2) slopes and should be small and light enough to pack, if necessary. Snowshoes work with any boot. (See figure 6-29.) 114 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-29. Snowshoes 6-96. Ski poles are typically used with snowshoes and skis to provide more lateral stability and balance. Ski poles can be used to provide excellent support for weapons systems during firing from the prone, kneeling, and standing positions. 6-97. Sleds are useful for carrying large amounts of equipment, such as bivouac equipment, heavy weapons, food and water, or other supplies. They range in size, shape, and weight, all of which should be considered before selection for military operations. Four- and ten-Soldier Ahkio-style sleds are available through the military supply system. These are designed to carry all group sustainment equipment (for example, tents, stoves, fuel) for a four- or ten-Soldier group. These come with a cover and rigid poles, convenient for dragging up and downhill. (See figure 6-30, page 116.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 115

Chapter 6 Figure 6-30. Ahkio sleds 6-98. Crampons attach to the Soldier’s boot to provide traction on ice and snow. There are two basic types: general mountaineering crampons and ice climbing crampons. Mountaineering crampons have less aggressive points. They are designed for use in steep snow and on low-angle ice and can be used for ice climbing but are not ideal. Ice climbing crampons have points that are more aggressive and are typically more rigid. They are designed for steep ice climbing but can be used in snow and low angle ice as well. Crampons work best when paired with a stiff leather or rigid plastic mountaineering boot. They do not work well with issued cold-weather combat boots. (See figure 6-31.) Figure 6-31. Crampons 6-99. Mountain axes are important tools for movement over steep snow and occasional low-angle ice. The two types of axes usually used in alpine terrain are general mountain axes and hybrid mountain axes. General axes are designed for steep snow and hybrid axes are designed for steep snow and low-angle ice climbing. Ice axes have an adze to the rear of the pick for chopping snow and ice. (See figure 6-32.) 116 TC 3-97.61 26 November

They are much more aggressive and curved to help obtain solid sticks in hard vertical ice and over bulges. They are less effective in snow than general or hybrid axes because of their short length. Ice tools can include an adze or a hammerhead. Hammers are used for placing pitons during mixed climbing. (See figure 6-33, page 118.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 117

Chapter 6 Figure 6-33. Ice tools MILITARY OPERATIONS IN SNOW- AND ICE-COVERED TERRAIN 6-101. Snow and ice present many additional challenges for units that need to move in mountainous terrain. Specialized equipment, training, and experience are necessary to move in it safely and effectively. Whether the challenges are deep snow, slick slopes, or steep sections of vertical ice, they will prove substantial obstacles for unprepared units. Units anticipating operating in such terrain and conditions should train in them prior to engaging in combat operations. 6-102. Even with proper equipment and training, it is unlikely that larger units can move in terrain steeper than 2nd-class terrain without ropes due to the high risk of long sliding falls. Small teams of advanced military mountaineers should be trained to move over ice and snow and tasked with finding routes and establishing rope systems for larger units. (See chapter 11 for establishing fixed-rope systems for troop movement in steep terrain and ATP 3-21.50 for crossing VDA TTP.) 118 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility MOVEMENT OVER SNOW 6-103. Low- to moderate-angle snow slopes found on or adjacent to valleys are primary avenues of movement for military units operating in winter conditions. Steeper slopes in gullies and passes are often the easiest routes through even steeper rocky features around them. Though challenging to move over, these often provide the best access to points of domination in alpine terrain. 6-104. Techniques for moving over snowy surfaces change IAW slope and surface conditions. Some soft snow increases physical strain but can increase the security of foot placements. During movement, breaks should be taken more frequently and for shorter durations in cold weather to assist with moisture management. This helps prevent overheating, which can cause problems once movements stop. Snow deeper than calf-height makes movement difficult without skis or snowshoes. Hard-packed snow slopes requiring special techniques and equipment or falls that could result in serious injury or death are likely. 6-105. A thorough analysis of avalanche threat should be conducted prior to moving over slopes that could be exposed to avalanche risk. Terrain at any risk for avalanche should be avoided. All Soldiers moving in potential avalanche terrain must be equipped with avalanche protective equipment and

threat should be conducted prior to moving over slopes that could be exposed to avalanche risk. Terrain at any risk for avalanche should be avoided. All Soldiers moving in potential avalanche terrain must be equipped with avalanche protective equipment and trained in its use, as well as avalanche response procedures. (See chapter 5 for more information on avalanche considerations.) BOOT PACKING 6-106. The boot-packing method requires the least amount of training and special equipment. The same techniques can be used in mountain walking; however, there is often less traction. During the boot-packing method, Soldiers move slower and minor slips and falls should be expected. In deeper soft snow, Soldiers should step in the tracks left by the Soldier in front of them. This packs them into hard steps and makes movement less difficult. Rotate lead Soldiers to prevent fatigue. 6-107. Crampons are strongly recommended for moving on hard-packed slopes. However, if crampons are not available, there are a few techniques to use to improve the security of foot placements. Step kicking involves kicking the toe or edge of the boot into the surface with each step creating a small depression, which improves traction. Mountain axes can be used as a

to use to improve the security of foot placements. Step kicking involves kicking the toe or edge of the boot into the surface with each step creating a small depression, which improves traction. Mountain axes can be used as a third point of contact, allowing the body to gain more traction. The axe is typically held by its head in the uphill hand, with the pick to the rear (cane position). Steps can be cut into the slope using the axe’s adze to improve foot placement security. (See figure 6-34, page 120.) This technique is effective for short distances but is very time-consuming. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 119

Chapter 6 Figure 6-34. Step cutting GLISSADING 6-108. Glissading is a technique used to descend low to moderate angle slopes by sliding in the seated position and using a mountain axe as a brake. (See figure 6-35.) Glissading allows Soldiers to descend appropriate slopes very quickly and efficiently, thereby saving significant time and energy. Specific conditions are required for glissading to be appropriate. The slope should not have any obstacles (such as trees, rocks, drop offs, crevasses) in the slide path, and it should have sufficient soft snow on the surface to allow Soldiers to control the speed of the slide. Glissading should never be done on hard-packed snow or ice surfaces. Crampons should be removed prior to glissading to ensure injuries to lower extremities are not caused by a crampon becoming caught on something during the slide. 6-109. Glissading is conducted by sitting in the snow and positioning the midpoint of a mountain axe shaft against one hip with the spike in the snow. The hand on the same side as the axe holds its shaft to the hip at the midpoint. The other hand holds the top of the axe where pick, shaft and adze meet. The mountain

the spike in the snow. The hand on the same side as the axe holds its shaft to the hip at the midpoint. The other hand holds the top of the axe where pick, shaft and adze meet. The mountain axe pick should always face forward (away from the Soldier) to prevent injury. Soldiers then initiate the slide on their buttocks using the axe spike as a brake. To slow down, Soldiers rotate the spike downward, pressing it deeper into the snowpack and increasing friction. To speed up, Soldiers rotate the spike away from the snowpack, decreasing friction. Adequate time should be allowed between Soldiers sliding in the same glissade path to ensure a collision does not occur should a Soldier stop shortly mid-slide. 120 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-35. Glissading FLATFOOTING 6-110. Flatfooting is the term for numerous techniques that increase security and efficiency of movement over snow and ice slopes. These techniques involve the use of both crampons and a mountain axe. The key principle of flatfooting is to position the body so that all crampon points are embedded in the snow surface. This provides maximum security for foot placements. These techniques are particularly critical to safe movement over steep, hard-packed snow. Flatfooting with heavy loads requires greater proficiency. Flatfooting techniques are much more difficult to perform in flexible boots or with loose sloppy crampons. There is little margin for error in executing self-arrest on steep slopes with firm surface conditions. Good movement skills are still the primary risk mitigation for moving unroped. 6-128. Soldiers should carry the axe in the cane position with the pick to the rear in the uphill hand. The instant Soldiers fall, they must commit to self-arresting immediately. The technique is executed by bringing the mountain axe into position at the center of chest, with the hand on its head and pick facing away. The lower hand moves to a position low on the axe shaft. Chapter 7 Navigation in Mountainous Terrain The goals, strategies, and tools available to Soldiers for navigation in mountainous terrain are no different from other types of terrain. However, mountainous terrain makes using those tools to stay on course much more difficult. Additionally, straying off course while navigating in this terrain can prove extremely hazardous and detrimental to mission success. The difficulty of planning routes and calculating movement timelines also increases significantly with the steepness and complexity of terrain. Soldiers and leaders who learn how to mitigate these challenges effectively can not only successfully navigate in mountainous terrain but also better use the terrain for cover and concealment. Navigation is the process of determining one’s present position, locating a target objective, and selecting and following a route between these two points. Navigation consists of three distinct stages: orientation, navigation, and route finding. 7-2. Orientation is simply figuring out exactly where one is. Using a map, compass, and identifiable terrain features, assisted by an altimeter and GPS, is the foundation of good orientation. 7-3. Route finding is picking the best line of travel IAW METT-TC (I); mission, enemy, terrain and weather, troops and support available, time available, civil considerations, and informational considerations, and the commander’s intent. ROUTE PLANNING 7-36. Careful map reconnaissance, knowledge of the enemy situation, terrain analysis of the operational area, and an accurate assessment of the unit’s capabilities are all key parts of the planning process. Route planning in the mountains proves to be difficult, and often the original route selection changes during movement due to the restrictive nature of this terrain. Always use METT-TC (I) to maximize advantages of routes used in military operations and carefully weigh costs and benefits of route decisions. Additionally, weather and surface conditions impact route decisions greatly. MISSION FACTORS 7-37. The mission and commander’s intent must be considered when planning routes in the mountains. Establish priorities for route characteristics IAW their impact on the mission. Some common examples of route selection priorities are navigability of terrain, tactical advantage or disadvantage throughout the movement, concealment throughout, fatigue reduction, and required speed of movement. Chapter 8 Knot Tying and Rope Management The rope is a vital piece of equipment to the mountaineer. It is used to address many of the problems and hazards encountered in the mountains. When climbing, rappelling, or building rope installations, the mountaineer must know how to utilize and maintain this equipment. Misuse can cause serious injury or death. This chapter discusses equipment, terminology, knots, hitches, rope management techniques, care, and maintenance. SECTION I – TYPES OF ROPE, WEBBING, AND CARABINERS 8-1. Mountaineering equipment is engineered to be lightweight but strong enough to provide a wide margin of safety. Each item is tested to high standards. In most cases, user error is to blame when this equipment fails. Soldiers should regularly check and inspect mountaineering equipment. Equipment should be replaced when there is any obvious damage, or it has exceeded the manufacturer’s lifecycle recommendation. 8-2. All mountaineering equipment used in training should be constructed and tested to a recognized standard. The International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation, or Union des International Alpine Association (UIAA), is the certifying body that defines the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment. This safety commission develops the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment recognized throughout the world.

International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation, or Union des International Alpine Association (UIAA), is the certifying body that defines the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment. This safety commission develops the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment recognized throughout the world. In Europe, the European Conformity, or Conformité Européene (CE), and the European Committee for Standardization establish standards across all industries. They publish standards that align with the UIAA standards for all climbing and mountaineering equipment produced in Europe. The United States has no specific standards, but American manufacturers have their equipment tested to receive UIAA certification. Any equipment used for mountaineering should be marked with either the UIAA safety label or the CE standard that it meets. ROPES AND CORDS 8-3. Ropes and cords are Soldiers’ lifelines in the mountains. Soldiers should understand the types of ropes and cords and their applications. All ropes and cords used in mountaineering and climbing today are constructed with the same basic configuration. Chapter 8 8-4. There are many types of fibers and ropes that each have unique characteristics, making them suitable for specific tasks. The two main categories of rope are static and dynamic. Military mountaineers need to be able to differentiate between the two and know how each rope should be used. STATIC ROPE 8-5. A static rope is a kernmantle rope designed for minimal stretch under load, primarily used for hauling, lowering, and anchor systems construction. It has a core (kern) that is laid straight, giving it low stretch (2 to 8 percent). They are constructed with a tightly woven sheath (mantle) and are more durable than dynamic ropes. Static ropes are preferred for rappelling, rescue operations, load hauling, and rope installations. They should never be used in situations where the rope is shock loaded (for example, lead climbing). Typical diameter for static rope is between 9 and 11 millimeters (mm). Static rope is issued in 600 feet (183 meters) spools. While the minimum tensile strength for static ropes for military use is 4,500 pounds, the recommended working load is often 25 percent of the actual strength of that rope. The tensile strength for the 9.5 mm-issued low-stretch kernmantle rope

The tensile strength for the 9.5 mm-issued low-stretch kernmantle rope is approximately 6,000 pounds. The length needed is dependent on the specific task being conducted. A 45-meter (150 feet) static has been the standard military length since the introduction of nylon ropes, but some tasks or obstacles may require a longer rope. The length of rope over 100 meters is a challenge to carry and manage. 8-6. A rope of unknown history or construction should not be used for any application. DYNAMIC ROPE (CLIMBING ROPE) 8-7. A dynamic rope is a kernmantle rope designed to stretch and absorb force, primarily used to protect climbers from fall injuries. All climbing should be protected with dynamic ropes. SECTION II – BASIC TERMINOLOGY 8-19. Understanding basic terminology is important when learning how to tie knots. The terms explained in this section are the most common in military mountaineering. (See figure 8-6, page 156.) RUNNING END 8-20. A running end is the loose or working end of the rope. STANDING END 8-21. The standing end is the static, stationary, or nonworking end of the rope. 154 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Knot Tying and Rope Management BIGHT 8-22. A bight of rope is a bend in the rope in which the standing end is parallel to the running end and the rope does not cross itself. LOOP 8-23. A loop is a bend of the rope in which the rope crosses itself. When the running end crosses over the top of the standing end, it is an overhand loop. When the running end crosses under the standing end, it is an underhand loop. TURN 8-24. A turn wraps around an object, providing 360° contact. ROUND TURN 8-25. A round turn wraps around an object one and one-half times so that the running and standing end are parallel. A round turn is used to hold an anchor or knot in place. HALF HITCH 8-26. A half hitch is a turn with the running end crossing over the standing end. TAIL 8-27. The tail is the excess portion of the running end of the rope when the knot is completed. If a knot requires an overhand safety, the length of the tail is measured from the safety knot to the end of the rope. A safety knot is a backup knot tied to

the rope when the knot is completed. If a knot requires an overhand safety, the length of the tail is measured from the safety knot to the end of the rope. A safety knot is a backup knot tied to prevent a primary knot from slipping loose. DRESSING 8-28. Dressing a knot is arranging all the knot parts, removing unnecessary kinks, twists, and slack so that all rope parts of the knot are secured and tight. SETTING 8-29. Setting a knot is removing all unnecessary slack from the knot. This ensures that the knot is tight and minimizes the chances of the knot becoming untied. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 155

Chapter 8 Figure 8-6. Examples of rope-tying terminology SECTION III – KNOT TYING AND CONSIDERATIONS 8-30. The term knot is commonly used to describe numerous categories. A knot is the fixed portion of a rope that has been manipulated around itself, another object, or both during the process of being tied for some purpose. Sometimes it is referred to as a “hard knot” since its condition will remain intact until actively untied. Knots are self-contained and self-supporting and do not need another object or rope to maintain its integrity. Hitches are not considered knots. Yet, for simplicity, they are generalized into a single category. Knots should never be considered permanent. It is possible that they can loosen or become less secure under certain conditions. Knots should be inspected regularly. Many knots can accomplish the same task; therefore, it is important to understand these considerations when choosing the appropriate knot to tie. to be able to tie every possible knot that can be used in mountaineering. They just need to be able to tie an appropriate knot for each application they may face in their duties. The service life of a rope depends on the frequency of use, applications (rappelling, climbing, rope installations), speed of descent, surface abrasion, terrain, climate, and quality of maintenance. Chapter 9 Anchor Selection and Construction Understanding anchors is an important fundamental that must be understood early in the path to becoming a military mountaineer. An anchor is the point where manufactured equipment for mountaineering meets the surface of the earth. Great varieties of natural features are found in different operational environments that a Soldier could use to construct an anchor. Anchors are found in all rope systems and are built in many ways. This chapter gives Soldiers the tools to assess terrain for the suitability of anchor construction for a wide variety of rope systems. This chapter also exposes Soldiers to the principles of anchor construction that ensure they are building solid anchors in a wide variety of terrain for many different purposes. Anchor selection in mountainous terrain requires a certain degree of knowledge and substantial experience. Most mountaineering accidents occur at the anchor. Inexperienced Soldiers should stick to selecting anchor features that are obviously stronger than necessary and choose simple rigging techniques with which they are familiar. SECTION I – GENERAL PRINCIPLES: SINGLE AND MULTIPOINT 9-1. An anchor for military mountaineering is a fixed object to which a rope system is secured and is of sufficient size, weight,

choose simple rigging techniques with which they are familiar. SECTION I – GENERAL PRINCIPLES: SINGLE AND MULTIPOINT 9-1. An anchor for military mountaineering is a fixed object to which a rope system is secured and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. It is a point in the operational environment, which a rope installation is attached, providing more than enough resistance to a directional pull. Rope systems can be used for moving casualties and equipment. Some, like rappels or fixed ropes, are used for aiding movement. Technical rope systems provide the tools for addressing many of the challenges posed by mountainous terrain. Anchor selection and evaluation together form the foundation of all systems. 9-2. Considerations for selecting a natural feature to construct an anchor are its location and ability to resist any forces that are placed upon it. The anchor should be above any intended rope pathways. This reduces the pendulum effect on any loads attached to the anchor. Another important facet of anchor location is its proximity to the edge. In some situations, having the anchor a short distance away from the edge creates a platform

This reduces the pendulum effect on any loads attached to the anchor. Another important facet of anchor location is its proximity to the edge. In some situations, having the anchor a short distance away from the edge creates a platform to work on. In other situations, such as setting a top rope, it is best to have the anchor near the edge. This aspect of anchor building can be challenging as the strength of natural features, such as rocks, trees, roots, and boulders; can be difficult to judge. Soldiers must err on the side of caution and leave no doubt that an anchor is strong enough for its intended purpose. If there is any doubt about a single-point anchor’s strength or security, then additional anchor components should be constructed and incorporated until sufficient strength and security are achieved to ensure that anchor failure cannot occur. The strength of an anchor should never be in question. 9-3. Anchors in mountaineering should be loaded in a steady and slow manner. Avoid bouncing as much as possible as it could weaken the integrity of the natural object being used. Sometimes slack can generate in various types of rope systems and cause an anchor

be loaded in a steady and slow manner. Avoid bouncing as much as possible as it could weaken the integrity of the natural object being used. Sometimes slack can generate in various types of rope systems and cause an anchor to be shock loaded. It is best to avoid any circumstances that may lead to this as shock loading results in very high forces on the anchor. SINGLE-POINT ANCHORS 9-4. Single-point anchors are the simplest in mountaineering and serve as the building blocks for more complicated anchors. If a single feature, object, or piece of equipment is to be used as an anchor, there must be no doubt that it is both strong enough and secure enough to hold if shock loading were to occur. The same goes for all rigging used in building the anchor. Correctly tied master points, locking carabiners, and double nonlocking carabiners opposite and opposed must be used for all points of connection. Anchor Selection and Construction SELF-EQUALIZING ANCHORS 9-15. A self-equalizing anchor is a multipoint anchor comprised of adjustable strands from each anchor component to a shared attachment point that allows for maximum load sharing even when direction of pull changes during use. (See figure 9-6, page 202.) Anchor Selection and Construction PRE-EQUALIZED ANCHORS 9-16. A pre-equalized anchor is the preferred type of multipoint anchor used in mountaineering. The anchor distributes the weight of the load among each individual anchor component using fixed and independent strands. (See figure 9-7.) Multipoint anchors orient all strands together pointing in the direction that the anchor will be loaded. A pre-equalized anchor prevents extending and shock loading the anchor if an individual component fails. An anchor is pre-equalized by tying a master point using an appropriate loop knot in the webbing or sling. 9-17. The mnemonic EARNEST-H can be used as a guide to build optimal and efficient multipoint anchors. Multipoint anchors should be— • E—equalized: Each component of the anchor shares the load evenly. Nonlocking carabiners are typically acceptable links between soft materials here. • A—angle: The angles between the strands of individual components should not exceed 90°, if possible. The goal is to minimize multiplying forces as shown in figure 9-7. • R—redundant: The entire anchor system is not reliant on a single anchor component. Rigging of the cord is such that if a single strand breaks or is cut, the entire anchor would not fail. Redundancy is achieved by

Chapter 9 SECTION II – TREES 9-18. Tree anchors should be considered for use first. They are usually strong and often simple to construct with minimal use of equipment. Trees are already in place and simply require a method of attaching the rope. However, they should be carefully studied and evaluated for stability and strength before use. Sometimes the rope is tied directly to the anchor, but under most circumstances, a cord or sling is attached to the tree and then the climbing rope is attached to the sling with a carabiner. A high-strength tie off is a single-point anchoring method that retains maximum installation rope strength and releasability, using multiple-round turns around the anchor object to create friction, and securing the end back to itself ensuring no force is applied to any component knots or carabiners. It is used to anchor the rope on high-load installations used for bridging and traversing. (See figure 9-9, page 206.) The wraps of the rope around the anchor absorb the tension of the installation and keep the tension off the knot and carabiner. The anchor is usually tied with a minimum of three wraps, more, if necessary, to absorb the tension. A smooth anchor may require several wraps, whereas a rough barked tree might only require a few. The rope is wrapped from top to bottom without crossing strands so that it can be untied under tension, if desired. A fixed loop is placed into the end of the rope and attached loosely back onto the rope with a locking carabiner. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 205

If viable, they provide one of the more secure natural anchor points as they can be pulled in any direction (See figure 9-12.) A natural anchor is a natural fixed object (such as a tree, rock formation, or ice formation) to which a rope system can be secured and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. A sling is threaded through the opening hole and secured with a joining knot or girth hitch. The load-bearing hole must be strong and free of sharp edges (pad, if necessary). A pinch-point anchor is used the same way as arches or tunnels; it is just formed by a pinch point between two large boulders, allowing a sling or cordelette to be tied around it. Boulders comprising a pinch point need to be large enough and secure enough to ensure they do not move when a force is applied. Sometimes a little digging in snow or earth provides a pinch-point anchor where no other options are available.

Artificial rock protection is anything used to protect a climber or anchor a rope system and is not part of the natural environment. The evolution of artificial protection started with handmade pieces of metal called pitons. Now there are several companies that manufacture various lightweight artificial protection. There is fixed and removable protection. Fixed protections are bolts and pitons; they are left in the rock for future use 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 209

Chapter 9 and can be difficult to remove. Removable protection refers to spring-loaded camming devices (known as cams), chocks, and other specialty protection that is easily recoverable after use. 9-28. Artificial protection is used to construct anchors in various ways. Anchors may be comprised of a combination of artificial protection and other objects, such as a tree or a boulder. The combinations are endless. However, when building anchors made with only artificial protection, multiple pieces are required. No single piece of artificial protection is considered adequate to comprise an anchor. A minimum of two components are needed to provide redundancy in the case of bad placement, poor rock quality, or any other factor causing a piece to fail. PITONS 9-29. Pitons have been in use for over 100 years. Although still available, pitons are not used as often as other types of artificial anchors due primarily to their impact on the environment. Most climbers prefer to use other artificial anchors rather than pitons because they do not scar the rock and are easier to remove. Pitons still have a place in military mountaineering since they are a relatively light, cheap, and expendable yet extremely strong and secure anchor option when

rather than pitons because they do not scar the rock and are easier to remove. Pitons still have a place in military mountaineering since they are a relatively light, cheap, and expendable yet extremely strong and secure anchor option when placed properly. They are particularly useful during rocky alpine descents, when an ice axe with a hammer is already carried and natural rappel anchors are scarce. 9-30. One piton is not considered strong or secure enough to serve as a single belay or system anchor. When establishing an anchor using multiple pitons, they should be placed in different cracks or features. A single piton can also be combined with other viable natural anchoring methods, if available. Note. Properly placing pitons requires significant practice to master, which should be conducted in training scenarios involving backup systems to protect the trainee should a placement fail. ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES 9-31. Some advantages with using pitons are— • Depending on type and placement, pitons can support multiple directions of pull. • They are less complex than other types of artificial anchors. • Pitons work well in thin cracks where other types of artificial anchors do not. 9-32. They are prohibited in most established climbing areas. • Pitons are easily dropped if not tied off when being used. PITON PLACEMENT 9-33. Properly positioning or placing pitons is critical. (See figure 9-13 for examples of piton placement.) Usually, a properly sized piton for a rock crack will fit one-half to two-thirds into the crack before being driven with the piton hammer. This helps ensure the depth of the crack is adequate for the size piton selected. Test the rock for soundness by tapping with the hammer. Driving pitons in soft or rotten rock is not recommended. When this type of rock must be used, clear the loose rock, dirt, and debris from the crack before driving the piton completely in. 9-35. While it is being driven, attach the piton to a sling with a carabiner (an old carabiner should be used, if available) so that if the piton is knocked out of the crack, it is not lost. The greater the resistance overcome while driving the piton, the stronger and more secure the anchor is. The quality of the rock around the crack a piton is placed into also greatly affects the strength and security of the anchor. Chapter 9 BOLTS 9-39. A bolt is a type of rock protection or anchoring component comprised of an expansion bolt or glue-in shaft attached to a hanger to which a carabiner can be attached. Bolts are often used in fixed-rope installations and in aid climbing where cracks are not available. Bolts provide one of the most secure means of establishing protection. 9-40. Some bolts have rings attached for easy retrievable rappelling, clip-in points for top rope climbing, chains to aid in establishing tope rope climbing anchors, or other special-purpose attachment points. 9-41. There are two primary types of bolts: expansion bolts and glue-in bolts. Both involve drilling a hole into a rock face, cleaning out dust and debris, and inserting a bolt. The difference is in how the bolt is secured in the hole: • Expansion bolts use a sleeve that expands as it is tightened. The sleeve expands against the walls of the hole to prevent it from coming out. (See figure 9-16.) • Glue-in bolts are held in place by a high-strength adhesive. Glue-in bolts are used in softer, porous rock, such as sandstone. Delicate rock, like sandstone, may not be strong enough to support expansion bolts. Its

Delicate rock, like sandstone, may not be strong enough to support expansion bolts. Its porous structure allows the glue to expand deep into the rock around the original hole. (See figure 9-17, page 216.) 214 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Chapter 9 Figure 9-17. Glue-in bolt ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES 9-42. Some advantages of using bolts in anchor construction are— • Extremely strong and secure when installed properly. • Very easy to use for climbing protection when already installed. • Very easy to use in multipoint-anchor construction when already installed. 9-43. Some disadvantages of using bolts in anchor construction are— • Extremely time consuming to install relative to other artificial anchoring devices. • Require the mountaineer to use both hands and hang during installation. • Require special, relatively heavy tools (for example, drills, hammers, wrenches) to install. • Noisy to install. 216 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Anchor Selection and Construction INSTALLATION AND USE 9-44. There are enough differences in bolts available on the market that mountaineers should refer to manufacturers’ instructions for installing bolts. Installing bolts permanently alters the rock. The climbing community has strong ethics regarding the placement of bolts. Ethics and regulations vary regionally, but in all areas, it is unacceptable to add bolts to existing climbs. Any bolting should be done with the consensus of the climbing community. 9-45. When using existing bolts as climbing protection or as part of an anchor system, mountaineers should inspect them for anything indicating compromise. The first thing that should be inspected is the rock on which it will be placed. Bolts are only as strong and secure as the quality of the rock. The hanger should not be rusty or loose. Loose hangers can indicate the bolt being insecure, or the hole has not been drilled deep enough to secure the hanger to the rock’s face. If the nut holding a hanger can be tightened to a point, then it is viable. If it keeps spinning, the bolt should not be used or at the very least backed up with additional protection. 9-46. Many chock picks

Many chock picks (sometimes referred to as nut-tools) have a hex cut out in them that can be used like a wrench to tighten loose bolts. The principles for using devices commonly called chocks, nuts, or stoppers are the same as with chockstones above. They are designed to work in smaller cracks, easier to place, and more secure. (See figure 9-19, page 218.) The direction of pull must be considered carefully when using chocks. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 217

Chapter 9 Figure 9-19. Chocks ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES 9-48. Using chocks in anchor construction has the following advantages: • Tactically quiet installation and recovery. • Usually easy to retrieve and, unless severely damaged, are reusable. • Light to carry. • Minimal rock scarring as opposed to pitons. • Sometimes can be placed where pitons cannot (expanding rock flakes where pitons would further weaken the rock). 9-49. Using chock in anchor construction has the following disadvantages: • May not fit in thin cracks, which may accept pitons. • Often provide only one direction of pull. • Practice and experience are necessary to become proficient in proper placement and removal. PLACEMENT 9-50. The principles of placing chocks are to find a crack with a constriction at some point, place a chock of appropriate size above and behind the constriction, and set the chock by gently jerking down. Maximum surface contact with a tight fit is critical. Chocks are usually good for a single direction of pull. 9-51. Avoid cracks that have crumbly (soft) or deteriorating rock, if possible. Some cracks may have loose rock, grass, and dirt, which should be removed before placing the chock. Look for a constriction point in the

single direction of pull. 9-51. Avoid cracks that have crumbly (soft) or deteriorating rock, if possible. Some cracks may have loose rock, grass, and dirt, which should be removed before placing the chock. Look for a constriction point in the crack, and then select a chock to fit it. 9-52. When selecting a chock, choose one that has as much surface area as possible in contact with the rock. A chock resting on one small crystal or point of rock is likely to be unsafe. A chock that sticks partly out of the crack is avoided. 9-53. All chocks used for lead climber protection should include a soft material extension, such as a runner, to prevent the rope from wiggling the chock out of placement. 218 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Anchor Selection and Construction 9-54. Chocks must be lightly tugged on to set them so that they do not fall out of placement. Weighting the placement helps to keep the protection in position. A carabiner often provides enough weight. CAMMING DEVICES 9-55. Camming devices are designed for building anchors in parallel-sided cracks where chocks are ineffective. There are several different types, but they all work by changing from a downward force to an outward force when loaded. This force creates enough friction that the device cannot move, even when no constriction in the crack is present. Camming devices increase force on surrounding rock as downward force is applied. Due to this, care should be taken to inspect the security of the rock on which they are placed. 9-56. Camming devices become even more secure when placed above a constriction. If the lobes slip during loading, they cannot exit the crack. 9-57. Cams are the most used camming devices in mountaineering. They have advantages and disadvantages and require extensive practice and experience to place and use properly. SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES 9-58. Cams are the most versatile and widely used artificial rock anchoring devices available to mountaineers. Although there are several types

They have advantages and disadvantages and require extensive practice and experience to place and use properly. SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES 9-58. Cams are the most versatile and widely used artificial rock anchoring devices available to mountaineers. Although there are several types of cams, the modern design consists of two sets of lobes that oppose each other and rotate from one or two axles, connected to a trigger mechanism on a single, flexible stem that runs perpendicular to the axle. Attached to the axle is a presewn connection sling. They are designed to work in parallel-sided cracks where a chock would just slide down. 9-59. Cams come in a wide variety of sizes to fit cracks from 0.5 inches to over 21 inches. Each unit has an expansion range that enables it to function properly within a certain width of cracks. It may be necessary to carry many sizes depending upon the route, mission, and intended use. Most come with color-coded slings to help the user select the correct size for use. 9-60. Three quality camming devices equalized together are required to establish an adequate anchor. An exception is two large camming devices perfectly placed in solid rock with constrictions below them.

An exception is two large camming devices perfectly placed in solid rock with constrictions below them. A single camming device is usually placed for intermediate lead-climbing protection. Suboptimal placements or rock features require additional pieces to achieve an acceptable anchor. ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES 9-61. The advantages of using cams in anchor construction are listed below: • They are much faster to place and remove, for creating anchors or as points of protection while lead climbing. • They require only one hand to place, so the mountaineer can hold on to the rock with the other. • They are easy to insert and remove when placed properly. • They can be more forgiving than other anchor devices if the direction of pull changes. • They provide many possibilities for rigging multipoint anchors. • They do not damage the surrounding rock. 9-62. The disadvantages of using cams in anchor construction are listed below: • They can wiggle or walk out of proper placement, resulting in a compromised anchor, or in a stuck camming device that is difficult or

the surrounding rock. 9-62. The disadvantages of using cams in anchor construction are listed below: • They can wiggle or walk out of proper placement, resulting in a compromised anchor, or in a stuck camming device that is difficult or impossible to remove. • They are much more expensive compared to other types of anchors. • They can be heavy and bulky to carry. • They have the potential to generate enough outward mechanical force to damage the surrounding rock and compromise the anchor when loaded. PLACEMENT 9-63. To place cams, find a uniform, parallel spot in the crack where the rock is clean and solid. Retract the lobes by pulling back on the trigger. Gently insert the camming device and release the trigger so the lobes expand to fit the crack. The spring mechanism works to hold the camming device in place. Avoid overcamming, which can make the unit difficult or impossible to remove, or undercamming, which results in too little surface area contact and reduced stability. The unit should also be placed deep enough to not break the edge of the crack but not so deep that the trigger mechanism cannot be reached. 9-65. Orient the stem to point in the direction from which the camming device is loaded. 9-66. Inspect the final placement to ensure the angle of the lobes in relation to each other is even and within the acceptable range. 9-67. An extension using a runner may be added between the camming device and climbing rope to reduce likelihood it walks out of position during lead climbing. 9-68. Single cam placements can be used for fall protection while lead climbing. Multiple cam placements can be equalized together with cordage or webbing to create load-bearing anchors. 9-69. Chapter 9 Figure 9-21. Cord anchor with multiple points SECTION IV – ICE ANCHORS 9-70. Fall protection and anchors can be constructed in alpine or waterfall ice using specialized ice screws. Occasionally, natural ice features can be found allowing anchor construction without them. TYPES OF ICE ANCHORS 9-71. Ice anchors consist of ice pillars, ice screws, and V-threads. Except for the case of large ice pillars, ice anchors should incorporate two or more anchor points to be strong and secure enough. ICE PILLARS, ICE SCREWS, AND V-THREADS 9-72. Ice pillars often form in steep alpine terrain. It is sometimes possible to pass a length of cordage or webbing around the whole mass of ice and create a single-point anchor in the same fashion as a rock protrusion or tree. (See figure 9-22.) Ice pillars should be totally frozen to the ground, comprised of dense, 222 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Anchor Selection and Construction crack-free ice, and greater than 1 foot in diameter to use as a single-point anchor. Smaller pillars may be used as part of multi-point anchors. 9-73. Occasionally, ice pillars can be created in ice features, such as sufficiently thick ice curtains where there is a hollow space behind, and a hole can be broken through a thin section with a mountain ax. Then an anchor can be established as above. Care must be taken not to damage the selected ice mass when creating a hole. Figure 9-22. Ice pillar ICE SCREWS 9-74. The ice screw is the most common type of ice protection. An ice screw is a threaded tubular screw with teeth on the end. Some screws have longer hangers or handles, which allow them to be easily twisted into position by hand. Ice screws come in various lengths for use in various ice thicknesses. Newer ice screws come manufactured with a twist knob on the hanger for easier placement. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 223

Chapter 9 9-75. The security of an ice screw is determined by the quality of the ice in which it is placed. The thicker and denser the ice is, the stronger it is. Thinner ice, aerated ice, or ice with air pockets is weak; mountaineers should avoid this sort of ice. Deep, thick ice is generally bluish in color, while ice that has air pockets is often white in color. It takes significant experience to judge the strength of ice, but even a novice can learn much about ice quality by the resistance felt when placing the ice screw. Air pockets are felt as a reduction in resistance. The more resistance, the denser the ice. The longer the core grows as it is screwed in, typically the better the ice. (See figure 9-23.) Evaluate the integrity of the ice structure. If possible, avoid fracture lines, the apex of ice bulges, and ice blocks that are not attached to a main flow. Figure 9-23. Long ice core protruding from screw indicates good ice quality 9-76. One ice screw in quality ice is sufficient to protect a lead climber. Two or more ice screws must be placed in quality ice to create

flow. Figure 9-23. Long ice core protruding from screw indicates good ice quality 9-76. One ice screw in quality ice is sufficient to protect a lead climber. Two or more ice screws must be placed in quality ice to create a secure anchor. (See figure 9-24.) The same principles apply for creating multipoint anchors for ice screws. If the ice quality is suboptimal, then additional screws should be incorporated. 224 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Hold the hanger end of the screw, and press teeth against the surface at an approximately 90° angle to the ice with a twisting motion. An acceptable range is +/–20°. (See figure 9-25, page 226.) Typically, several twists are necessary to get it started. The screw is started when it does not fall out of the ice. Chapter 9 Figure 9-27. Constructing a V-thread anchor SECTION V – EARTH ANCHORS 9-93. Using improvised earth anchors becomes necessary when naturally existing anchors, such as trees, are unavailable. These anchors are created using materials that are readily available. The strength of these anchors depends on the material used, the depth, and the density of the earth in which they are placed. The art of constructing and placing good earth anchors requires a great deal of practice and experience. It is especially important to load earth anchors in a slow and steady manner. It is also important to ensure the direction of the pull is low and does not pull up on any component of the earth anchor. DEADMAN ANCHOR 9-94. A deadman is an effective means of building an anchor in earth or snow when there are no other natural anchors available. A deadman is constructed by digging a trench perpendicular to the direction of pull and placing a lengthy solid object with a sling or cordelette attached into it. A thinner slot is cut into the ground in the direction of pull and bisecting the trench to form a T-shape. The attached cordelette or webbing is then routed

lengthy solid object with a sling or cordelette attached into it. A thinner slot is cut into the ground in the direction of pull and bisecting the trench to form a T-shape. The attached cordelette or webbing is then routed through this slot in the direction of pull. 9-95. The object is then buried. A rope or rope system can then be attached to it. The strength of a deadman anchor is determined by the density of soil it is placed into. The security of it is determined by the depth of the trench. Objects such as lengthy rocks, sticks, poles, and mountain axes can be buried. PICKET HOLDFAST 9-96. A picket holdfast can be constructed in the absence of suitable existing anchors. It requires three suitable pickets that can be made from sturdy sticks at least 3 inches in diameter and 3-feet long. The pickets can also be improvised from sturdy metal stakes or poles, if available. It is best to sharpen one end of each wooden stick or picket, so they are easily driven into the ground. (See figure 9-28.) 9-97. Next, drive the pickets in line with the load a safe distance from the edge. Drive the

Next, drive the pickets in line with the load a safe distance from the edge. Drive the pickets approximately 2-feet apart from each other at a 45° angle leaning away from the edge. The pickets should be driven into the ground at least half their total length. 9-98. Attach the rear picket at its base with a cord. Then attach the other end at the top of the middle picket. Using a clove hitch here will make it easy to adjust so there is equal tension on the pickets. 9-99. Two or more snow anchor points can be equalized into a multipoint anchor if strength and security are questionable. PICKETS AND ICE AXES 9-101. Pickets and ice axes may be used as snow anchors. The picket should be driven into the snow at 10° to 15° off perpendicular from the lower surface. If the picket cannot be driven in all the way to the top hole, the carabiner should be placed in the hole closest to the snow surface to reduce leverage. The picket may also be tied off with a short loop of webbing or rope girth hitched low on the picket. (See figure 9-29, page 230.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 229

Chapter 9 Figure 9-29. Snow picket placement 9-102. When the snowpack is loose or it is suspected that a single picket cannot act as a sufficient anchor, then use multiple pickets if available. (See figure 9-30.) If the snow picket goes into the snow with ease, consider placing it in the deadman orientation to maximize strength and surface contact. If the snow picket requires pounding to place in vertically, the placement is most likely solid. The same general principles apply to constructing this multipoint anchor as any other. Ensure that each picket shares the load equally. They can be placed in succession similarly to the picket holdfast described in section V in this chapter or in a reverse V-shape shown in figure 9-31, page 232. If the snow is extremely loose, it may be better to build a deadman anchor that is dug in quite deeply where there is firmer snow. 230 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

In softer snow conditions, both snow pickets and mountain axes can be used effectively in constructing a deadman anchor in the same fashion that they are constructed in earth (described in paragraphs 9-93 through 9-99, page 228). Longer objects, such as skis, can be used for increased strength. (See figure 9-31, page 232.) Snow density determines strength, and depth of the deadman determines security. Deadman anchors are the most reliable compared to all other techniques described. (See figure 9-31, page 232.)
