Chapter 10 Rope Systems for Climbing There is an inherent risk to moving in the mountains. Much of the terrain is high consequence, where a misjudged foothold, a loose rock, a slip, trip, or fall can kill. However, troops fighting in the mountains are often exposed to greater risk by not being able to move through the terrain. Examples exist throughout history. Modern examples include the assaults on Riva Ridge and Monte la Difensa in Italy, both examples of failed conventional assaults, where defensive positions in the heights were taken by assaults through more difficult terrain. More recently, the Indians retaking hilltops in the Kargil Conflict display all the same principles. Successful offensive operations in the mountains require troops who can move in difficult terrain and under poor conditions. The alternative is costly, often unsuccessful attacks where the defenders hold significant tactical advantage. To manage the risk involved with movement through these types of terrain, Soldiers must be trained in a variety of rope systems for climbing. SECTION I – RISK MITIGATION 10-1. Fighting in the mountains requires exposure to mountain hazards. The mountain environment is defined by its hazards and difficulties. Often, the control measures used to address one

a variety of rope systems for climbing. SECTION I – RISK MITIGATION 10-1. Fighting in the mountains requires exposure to mountain hazards. The mountain environment is defined by its hazards and difficulties. Often, the control measures used to address one hazard increase the exposure to another. Installing or using ropes to protect against a fall increases movement time and increases the exposure to compromise by enemy forces. MANAGING RISK 10-2. Managing risk in the mountains is a dynamic process, where the most appropriate measures for managing risk change with the terrain and situation. 10-3. Control measures target either the consequence or the likelihood of an incident. Protective equipment, such as a helmet to protect against rockfall, only reduces the consequence. The likelihood of being hit by rockfall is addressed by avoiding areas of loose rock and routing Soldiers so that they do not travel above one another. REDUCING THE LIKELIHOOD OF A FALL 10-4. The mountaineer has several technical tools for managing fall hazards. However, while the consequence of a fall can be reduced, it cannot be eliminated. Even a short fall while rock climbing can cause severe injury. To manage the risk, target factors that will reduce the likelihood

for managing fall hazards. However, while the consequence of a fall can be reduced, it cannot be eliminated. Even a short fall while rock climbing can cause severe injury. To manage the risk, target factors that will reduce the likelihood of a fall. JUDGEMENT 10-5. The safety of a mountaineer comes from the ability to read the terrain. Judge the rock, snow, or ice, and see where it can be climbed and where it cannot. This includes identifying features and weaknesses that can be linked together. Judgement is developed through time spent climbing in a controlled environment and through experience and mentorship. TECHNIQUE 10-6. Soldiers must possess the physical ability to make the moves, use footholds, and maintain balance as each move is made. As with judgement, climbing technique is the product of extensive training. LOAD 10-7. Increased Soldier load rapidly increases the difficulty of climbing, even in easy terrain. Operations in the mountains are subject to the mindset that occupying high terrain requires more equipment for sustaining life than at lower elevations. However, to maintain maneuverability, the Soldier’s load must be reduced. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 235

Chapter 10 Soldiers conducting offensive operations, reconnaissance patrols, or any maneuver in high-consequence terrain need to travel light. FOOTWEAR 10-8. Proper footwear will enhance the military mountaineer’s ability to move safely and efficiently through the rugged terrain found in the mountains. (See chapter 4 for footwear considerations.) ROPE 10-9. Ropes are used to reduce the consequence of a fall. Ropes can be fixed in place to manage or reduce the consequences of a fall (see chapter 11) or can be used to provide belays (see section III in this chapter). SECTION II – CONSIDERATIONS FOR MOVING UNROPED 10-10. Moving unroped is the fastest and most efficient method of moving through terrain. It requires little equipment and is quiet. Team members can move together, making communication quiet and easy. In instances where the greatest hazard is not falling, but rock or icefall, impending severe weather threat, enemy observation, or failing to meet an operational timeline, moving unroped may be the safest way to move. (See figure 10-1.) Moving unroped in terrain above 3rd-class should only be done after thorough risk analysis has been conducted and speed has been identified as a critical control measure for managing overall operational risk. SECTION III – BELAYED CLIMBING 10-13. A belay is a system of using a rope as a backup in steep terrain to arrest a Soldier’s fall should one occur. This section will discuss an overview of various strategies for using ropes and belays. TYPES OF BELAYED CLIMBING 10-14. When terrain is too dangerous to move unroped, a team will transition to belayed climbing. Belayed climbing is usually done in a party of two, with each climber tied into one end of the rope. One team member is always anchored and providing a belay for the other. TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-15. Military mountaineers are first introduced to top rope climbing. Top rope climbing is where the rope is run through

end of the rope. One team member is always anchored and providing a belay for the other. TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-15. Military mountaineers are first introduced to top rope climbing. Top rope climbing is where the rope is run through an anchor at the top of a climb and kept relatively snug to avoid longer falls. It is a training tool used to teach climbing technique. (See section IV for more information on top rope climbing.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 237

Chapter 10 LEAD CLIMBING 10-16. As military mountaineers progress, they are later introduced to lead climbing. Lead climbing is climbing a route while attached to the end of a rope to place devices in rock, ice, or snow for fall protection with a belayer located below. When lead climbing, one climber leads climbs, placing protection and clipping the rope through it as they go. The belayer (sometimes referred to as the second) belays and is prepared to catch a fall. Lead climbers climb to another secure stance, build a solid anchor, and then belay second climbers as they climb to the new stance. Each length of climbing is called a pitch, which is a section of a climb that comprises the distance between two belay stations, which can be up to a standard rope length (60 meters) on easy ice and snow. In more broken rock, it may be just 10 to 15 meters, to minimize rope drag and aid communication. 10-17. Lead climbing provides security for both members of the party. Leaders accept more risk because they are climbing above their protection. Any fall will be well past the last piece of protection they placed before the rope begins

communication. 10-17. Lead climbing provides security for both members of the party. Leaders accept more risk because they are climbing above their protection. Any fall will be well past the last piece of protection they placed before the rope begins to come tight, so it is still imperative that leaders have good movement skills. The second has a top rope unless the route traverses. The overall security of the team is good. The team always has a solid attachment, and the belays can be placed in sheltered stances, with solid anchors. (See section V for more information on lead climbing.) 10-18. Most climbers will protect themselves with belays in 5th-class terrain. In 3rd- or 4th-class terrain, in darkness or bad weather, belayed climbing is the most conservative strategy for protecting the team and provides the greatest margin of safety. AID CLIMBING 10-19. If the climbing is too difficult for the leader, aid climbing is a climbing technique in which standing on or pulling oneself up via devices attached to fixed or placed protection is used to make upward progress. Aid climbing is when climbers use anchors and protection to support their weight as they climb. In a recreational setting, climbers on big walls may do extensive aid climbing, with webbing ladders called etriers (or aiders) that can be clipped to pieces of rock protection and climbed, and daisy chains or webbing tethers, to hang from. Aid climbing can also be as simple as pulling on pieces of protection to get through difficult sections of what would otherwise be a free climb. 10-20. Aid climbing is slow. Simul-climbing is a belay technique involving two Soldiers climbing simultaneously while attached to the ends of a rope which runs through the fall protection. It is a variation of belayed climbing, where leaders continue to climb rather than stopping to belay the second. Second climbers climb simultaneously, removing protection as they go. Leaders continue to climb while trying to keep a few pieces of protection between the two climbers at all times. If one falls, they may pull their teammate off their stance, but they will be caught eventually, counterbalanced through the protection with the other climber. Simul-climbing is faster than belayed climbing and useful for covering easy ground quickly. (See figure 10-3, page 240.) Simul-climbing provides more security than soloing. Climbers may find it necessary to shorten ropes between 20 and 30 meters to help with communication and prevent rope drag. 10-22. When both climbers are moving together, both share the consequence of a fall. Climbers should only use simul-climbing where a fall is unlikely and with partners of similar ability. Rope Systems for Climbing Short Roping 10-24. Short roping is a technique that may have some use in training military mountaineers. (See figure 10-4, page 242.) Short roping is used by more experienced mountaineers for protecting less experienced Soldiers in easy but exposed terrain. The climbing rope is shortened to just a few meters, and the leader holds the rope close to the other’s harness and the two move together. Short roping cannot arrest a fall. It manages risk by putting the senior mountaineer close to the other climber, where the senior mountaineer can coach and model. If someone slips, leaders pull the rope connected to their harness to prevent the slip from becoming a fall. The only anchor is the senior mountaineer’s stance. Short roping is appropriate only in terrain where leaders are confident climbing unroped and do not need their hands to climb. 10-25. Short roping has limited application for military mountaineers. Short roping requires practice and the leader’s full attention. In an operational environment, the military mountaineer’s focus must be forward, looking for upcoming hazards or enemy contact. Often, because 4th-class terrain is more stepped, with plenty of ledges and stances, the leader can use simpler belay techniques and anchors than when rock climbing in 5th-class terrain and use a much shorter rope. 10-27. Most of the military mountaineer’s time is spent avoiding the steepest and most difficult terrain. Operationally, they are more likely to use terrain where short pitching and simul-climbing would be most efficient. Chapter 10 Figure 10-6. Kiwi coil OPERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS 10-32. The various strategies and techniques described above for moving while roped will compromise speed and security. In a training environment, safety and conservative decision making must be the primary focus. As military mountaineers progress in their training, they may be exposed to alpine terrain above tree line. Weather and environmental hazards can pose a greater threat than falling. Each strategy for protecting the movement of the team is a compromise that should match the difficulty of terrain and the consequence of a fall. It should not expose the team to greater risk from another hazard. For combat operations, military mountaineers may need to compromise on protection and belays even further. Speed, stealth, and the ability to react are critical if enemy contact is expected. SECTION IV – TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-33. A top rope is a belay in which both rope ends are on the ground and the rope runs up to the top of the cliff (or climb) and passes through a pre-established anchor point. This enables one Soldier to climb while the other Soldier belays. The belayer keeps the rope tight to prevent the climber from falling more than

to the top of the cliff (or climb) and passes through a pre-established anchor point. This enables one Soldier to climb while the other Soldier belays. The belayer keeps the rope tight to prevent the climber from falling more than a short distance. This system also enables the belayer to lower the climber back down to the ground after completing the climb. (See figure 10-7 for an example of top rope climbing.) 244 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Rope Systems for Climbing Figure 10-7. Top rope climbing 10-34. A top rope is a training tool. It allows Soldiers to learn the fundamentals of tying in and belaying and to practice individual climbing techniques without the consequences of a long leader fall or unroped fall. It allows one instructor to coach and supervise both the climber and the belayer. It also facilitates learning the climbing technique because all participants can observe one another. EQUIPMENT CONSIDERATIONS 10-35. The UIAA develops safety and testing standards for mountaineering equipment. Equipment used for any mountaineering training should meet these standards as outlined in chapter 8 and appendix C. HELMETS 10-36. Helmets will protect a Soldier from rockfall and debris. When worn, it should be tight around the waist, with the leg loops snug enough to take some of the force while falling or sitting into the harness. 10-39. They advise the commander on training requirements, priorities, and equipment needs, as well as plan, organize, and conduct training. SITE RECONNAISSANCE 10-44. Visit the training area before the scheduled training date and conduct a rehearsal or walkthrough with key personnel. This will help proof the plan, identify hazards, and develop controls. It is also an opportunity to save time with set up by identifying anchors and cleaning the area of loose rock or other hazards ahead of time. TIME MANAGEMENT 10-45. Climbs should be far enough apart so that climbers are not falling on or swinging into other climbers; however, they should not be so far apart that supervision and control are hindered. With climbs in close proximity, the instructor can often maintain adequate supervision of more than one climb. TRAINING SITE ANCHORS 10-55. Anchors at training sites are built stronger and more redundant than others used in climbing. A top roping anchor is used for long durations of time and is often out of the user’s sight. It either is loaded frequently, with climbers falling or as each climber is lowered back down to the ground. Extra care should be taken to avoid sharp edges and add padding where necessary. LOCATION OF ANCHORS 10-56. Anchors should be located directly above the climb. If the anchor is not above the climb, during a fall climbers will pendulum, swinging across the face until they are in line with the anchor. This is more pronounced the closer to the top the climber gets. CONSTRUCTION OF ANCHORS 10-57. Anchors must be strong and redundant. Developed climbing areas often have bolted anchors at the top of climbs.

The procedures for conducting a lead climb with a group of two are relatively simple. The most experienced individual is the lead climber or leader. Leaders are responsible for selecting the route. No matter how direct the route, the climber often encounters problems with rope drag through the protection positions. Rope drag is caused when there are exaggerated changes in direction of the rope between carabiners attached to protection that creates excessive friction. Minimal rope drag is an inconvenience; severe rope drag may pull the climber off balance, inducing a fall. When belaying the second, rope drag can be mistaken for the climber, causing the belayer to not take in the necessary slack. This can potentially result in a serious fall. To prevent this, the placements should be extended by using runners, when necessary, so the rope creates a smooth, almost straight line as it passes through the carabiners. (See figure 10-16.) Do this by attaching an appropriate-length runner to the protection to extend the rope connection in the necessary direction. The runner is attached to the protection while the rope is clipped into a carabiner at the opposite end of the runner. Rope Systems for Climbing On Ledges 10-110. On small or large ledges, it is usually possible to stack the rope in a neat pile as it is pulled through the belay. At hanging belay stances, it may be necessary to stack the rope back and forth over the tie-in strand as the Soldier pulls rope through the belay. If this is done, the rope should be looped back and forth in large bights (not so long as to becoming caught on things below). If the second becomes the new leader for the next pitch, these bights should start big and gradually become smaller. This allows the rope to feed out without becoming tangled during the next lead. If the original leader leads the next pitch, the rope may have to be restacked over the second’s tie-in strand when they reach the anchor. Another option is to stack the rope back and forth over a leg or foot. However, feet tend to get shifty when belaying during a long lead, which can lead to dropping the rope where it could possibly become stuck or jammed below.

Sometimes yelling cannot be heard when the climber and belayer are far apart. This is especially true in windy conditions or if the climber is around a corner, above an overhang, or at the back of a ledge. It may be necessary to use a series of tugs on the rope in place of the standard voice commands. To avoid any possible confusion with interpreting multiple rope tug commands, use only one. Chapter 10 SECTION VI – ALPINE BELAY TECHNIQUES 10-118. In broken alpine terrain, with secure stances, and no chance of second climbers falling and hanging from a belay, hasty techniques may provide adequate protection for the team. Safety should never be compromised for the sake of speed. Use of standard belay techniques should be used if there is any question as to security. BODY BELAYS 10-119. Body belays can sometimes be used on short sections of less steep terrain where a fall is unlikely and there is a good, braced belay stance of which to take advantage. To create a body belay, simply run the rope around the body at the waist to create friction, with the chest facing the direction of pull. The load rope is at one hip and the brake strand is in the opposite side hand. To take in rope, pull in on the load rope with the guide hand and out with the brake hand. Grab both ropes above the brake hand with the guide hand and slide the brake hand back towards the body. To brake, pull the brake hand up and across the chest. The body belay can be used in either the

Grab both ropes above the brake hand with the guide hand and slide the brake hand back towards the body. To brake, pull the brake hand up and across the chest. The body belay can be used in either the sitting or standing position; however, the sitting position offers a lower center of gravity and is preferred. It can also be used with an anchor or without. The advantage of the body belay is its speed and simplicity for belaying short sections where a climber is moving quickly. However, there are disadvantages as well. Because the force of a fall is dissipated as friction against belayers’ bodies, serious rope burns can occur to the body and hands, possibly causing them to lose control of the belay. It also generates less braking force and causes more slippage than other techniques, causing the climber to fall farther. For this reason, it is only used on low-angle easy terrain. The belayer must have a good, braced position and must keep the rope tight. (See figure 10-21.) 268 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Rope Systems for Climbing Figure 10-21. Hip belay SHOULDER BELAY 10-120. A shoulder belay is a way to add a level of friction to the rope as the belayer pulls it tight with a climber below. The shoulder belay shares many of the advantages and disadvantages listed above for the body belay. The level of friction created with this method is relatively low and should only be used on short steps where there is no risk of the climber hanging from the belay in a fall. A classic example of terrain where the shoulder belay is appropriate is a short, steep step where the belayer can stand directly above the climber below. The rope is routed under the arm, over the opposite shoulder, and down to the opposite hand and is kept tight with the climber below. The belayer’s body creates friction on the rope and acts as the anchor at the same time. A shoulder belay is fast to create, but it is only suitable on rare occasions. (See figure 10-22, page 270.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 269

The natural feature must be solid and not have sharp edges. Terrain belays are an effective means of belaying a climbing partner, but they require good judgement. When using a boulder or horn of rock, the belayer must ensure the rope will not slide off the rock in the event of a fall and that the rock is wedged securely. Trees are another good example of a natural object that can be used as a terrain belay. (See chapter 9 for more information on tree selection.) (See figure 10-23.) 270 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

To progress into managing two ropes, a climber must first become proficient in managing one. 10-123. It is good for military mountaineers to have options for roped travel through terrain with changing hazards. The mountaineer must constantly assess terrain and hazards and fluidly adapt the technique to mitigate those hazards as best as possible. Time is always against mountaineers, and efficient transitions from one roped movement style to the next are important. A mountaineer should not default to using one style of movement for all types of terrain and should know how to properly apply different roped movement techniques to different terrain. Chapter 11 Fixed Ropes Fixed ropes are an important part of military mountaineering as they facilitate the movement of Soldiers through rugged terrain. Fixed ropes allow large groups of Soldiers to safely access terrain that provides tactical advantage over the enemy. They have proven useful in past conflicts. During World War II, they were successfully used during Operation Neptune (commonly referred to as D-day) and the famous assault on Riva Ridge by the 10th Mountain Division. Proficiency in using fixed ropes allows units to overcome mobility limitations and, therefore, achieve greater lethality in mountainous terrain. SECTION I – BASIC FIXED-ROPE TECHNIQUES 11-1. A fixed rope is any rope system attached to at least one anchor that can be used to improve security and efficiency of movement through difficult terrain that subjects Soldiers to a fall hazard. They can be used for ascending, descending, or traversing across steep terrain in which a fall hazard exists. They may simply provide Soldiers with a handhold through a short section of steep terrain or as complex as hundreds of feet of broken hazardous terrain involving numerous sections that prevent attached Soldiers from being able to fall. They can be used to assist the movement

a handhold through a short section of steep terrain or as complex as hundreds of feet of broken hazardous terrain involving numerous sections that prevent attached Soldiers from being able to fall. They can be used to assist the movement of small teams to large units. They allow units to overcome mobility limitations and access tactically advantageous terrain. FIXED-ROPE CONSIDERATIONS 11-2. Fixed ropes should be used whenever a group of Soldiers cannot move safely through a section of terrain unroped. Fixed ropes are usually the most efficient means of protecting groups larger than team sized, especially if the groups have not received advanced military mountaineering training. Common factors contributing to the necessity of building fixed ropes are fall hazard, slippery surfaces, limited visibility, heavy loads, low mobility skills, and fatigue. 11-3. The two basic types of fixed-rope systems are simple fixed ropes and fixed ropes with intermediate anchors. Both types have applications in every class of terrain. Simple fixed ropes are anchored only at the top, can only be used by one Soldier at a time, and require a straight path of movement from bottom to top. Fixed ropes with intermediate anchors have multiple anchors and rope sections, allowing more

are anchored only at the top, can only be used by one Soldier at a time, and require a straight path of movement from bottom to top. Fixed ropes with intermediate anchors have multiple anchors and rope sections, allowing more Soldiers to move on them simultaneously and the path to change directions. Each type is determined by route and availability of anchors along it, the number of Soldiers to use the system, and the type of available equipment to attach to it. 11-4. All types of fixed ropes are built from the top down over, or through, terrain obstacles. However, fixed rope installation teams may need to ascend terrain using other techniques prior to building a fixed-rope system. (See chapter 10.) 11-5. Units planning to use fixed ropes must establish installation teams capable of locating routes, moving safely through various terrain obstacles, and building a variety of installations. They should be led by advanced military mountaineers but may be assisted by basic military mountaineers. These teams should be experienced in building fixed ropes in the type of terrain to be negotiated, equipped appropriately for the task, and familiar with the capabilities of the Soldiers who use them. 11-6. These teams should be experienced in building fixed ropes in the type of terrain to be negotiated, equipped appropriately for the task, and familiar with the capabilities of the Soldiers who use them. 11-6. In a tactical environment, any terrain that requires a fixed rope should be considered a VDA, which is steep terrain that puts a unit moving through it at significant tactical disadvantage. The process for establishing even the simplest fixed rope comes at the cost of time and exposure to enemy attack. Adequate security must be established prior to deploying the installation team. In complex terrain, security teams may need to be adjusted or leap-frogged forward if fixed-rope systems cover large pieces of terrain. Emplacing security teams in a complex terrain may require high-mobility skills as well as substantial time. Typically, it is best to approach fixed-rope terrain from above because security is more easily established on higher 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 275

Chapter 11 ground. But that is rarely possible. Units that anticipate building fixed-rope systems for movement in a combat environment should be well-rehearsed in crossing VDA TTP. (See ATP 3-21.50.) SIMPLE FIXED ROPES 11-7. A simple fixed rope is a rope that is anchored at the top of steep terrain that can be used to increase safety or efficiency of movement up or down. The method of anchoring the rope is determined by anchor features available but can be as simple as a bowline tied to a tree or as complex as a multipoint anchor established with rock-climbing gear. The principal benefit of simple, fixed ropes is their simplicity and speed of construction. 11-8. Simple fixed ropes are typically established by one mountaineer climbing the obstacle, dragging a rope, and then anchoring it at the top. They can also be established by approaching the top of a steep obstacle by some other means, anchoring a rope, and lowering the other end down for others to use. 11-9. Some important considerations for using simple fixed-rope systems are that they must follow a path straight up the terrain feature, the attachment technique is appropriate to reduce fall risk, and they allow for

end down for others to use. 11-9. Some important considerations for using simple fixed-rope systems are that they must follow a path straight up the terrain feature, the attachment technique is appropriate to reduce fall risk, and they allow for a large enough loading and unloading platform to manage the site safely. Using a friction hitch or mechanical progress capture to attach to the rope provides increased security during movement. EASY TERRAIN 11-10. Short 2nd- or 3rd-class slopes with low fall consequence can be negotiated using simple fixed ropes without the necessity of attaching to the rope. Soldiers using the fixed rope simply grasp the rope with the thumb downward and use it in a hand-over-hand fashion to assist with balance. (See figure 11-1.) This technique is appropriate when there is an increased likelihood of fall but low consequence. Usually this means short slopes that Soldiers could easily negotiate normally, but slippery conditions, fatigue, or heavy loads increase the chance of a fall. Knots can be added to increase the security of Soldiers moving on the rope, making it less likely their hand slips on the rope. Figure 11-1. Simple fixed rope use in easy terrain 276 TC 3-97.61 26

Fixed Ropes MODERATE TERRAIN 11-11. Short sections of steep 3rd or 4th class with higher fall consequence can be negotiated by attaching to simple fixed ropes with a progress capture, such as a prusik or other mechanical rope-grabbing device. This technique requires Soldiers to wear some type of harness. A significant drawback to this technique is that it takes a lot of time to move a group of Soldiers. Only one Soldier can move at a time on a rope, and time is lost during attachment and detachment. (See figure 11-2, page 278.) Prusik Technique 11-12. A common technique involves tying a prusik on the rope with a cordelette, then tying a fixed loop in the other end of the two tails. Clip the fixed loop to the harness with a locking carabiner. The optimum length of the attachment is one outstretched arm. 11-13. Ascend the fixed rope by using the legs to climb the slope and the rope as a handhold for balance, sliding the prusik up to capture progress and prevent fall in case of a slip. 11-14. The prusik technique is recommended only on simple fixed ropes without intermediate anchor points because friction hitches cannot be easily

a handhold for balance, sliding the prusik up to capture progress and prevent fall in case of a slip. 11-14. The prusik technique is recommended only on simple fixed ropes without intermediate anchor points because friction hitches cannot be easily or safely transitioned past intermediate anchors. Mechanical Ascender Technique 11-15. It is also possible to use a rope-grabbing device, such as a mechanical ascender, to create a progress capture for Soldiers moving on fixed ropes. These devices are easier and faster to use but require every Soldier to carry a piece of equipment that has limited uses. They should be used when fixed rope ascents are planned for large groups in moderate terrain. 11-16. Mechanical ascenders are devices shaped like a handle that can be attached to a rope by means of a toothed cam. It can slide in one direction on a rope but not the other. When weighted, the camming mechanism activates and grips the rope. Soldiers can attach ascenders to their harness and slide them along fixed ropes during movement, capturing their progress and preventing a fall during a slip (see figure 11-2, page 278). Ascenders should never be dynamically loaded as their teeth could damage the

attach ascenders to their harness and slide them along fixed ropes during movement, capturing their progress and preventing a fall during a slip (see figure 11-2, page 278). Ascenders should never be dynamically loaded as their teeth could damage the rope. Ascenders are included in the Army ACTK, but Solders can use other similar ascenders to ascend fixed ropes. Some are much lighter but are less easy to use. Advanced military mountaineers should familiarize themselves with the options available and units should obtain those best suited to the mountaineering tasks they must perform. 11-17. To use a mechanical ascender, attach it to the fixed rope. Then girth hitch a sling to the harness and clip it to the ascender with a locking carabiner. (See figure 11-2, page 278.) 11-18. Moving on simple fixed ropes in terrain where significant sections are very steep or vertical requires rigging that is more complex. These rigging techniques provide secure attachment to the rope and aid movement up the rope. (See paragraphs 11-36 through 11-52, pages 282 through 286, for more information on ascending techniques.) FIXED ROPES WITH INTERMEDIATE ANCHORS 11-20. Larger or more complex sections of steep terrain require fixed ropes with intermediate anchors to ensure adequate safety and efficiency of movement. This may involve various sections of 3rd, 4th, or even 5th-class terrain. The principal difference between simple fixed ropes and fixed ropes with intermediate anchors is the use of intermediate anchor points to create independent sections and changes in direction of travel. This allows the movement route to follow the easiest, safest, and most efficient path. This type of fixed rope is commonly used along exposed ridges and narrow mountain passes. 11-21. Advanced or master military mountaineers with substantial experience are required to establish fixed ropes with intermediate anchors, but they can be assisted by basic military mountaineers. narrow mountain passes. 11-21. FIXED-ROPE CONSTRUCTION WITH INTERMEDIATE ANCHORS 11-22. The primary guiding principles for building a fixed rope with intermediate anchors are that they provide adequate fall prevention while maximizing the speed at which Soldiers can move using them. Path 11-23. Establishing a fixed rope with intermediate anchors starts with thorough terrain analysis and route finding. When selecting a path for the rope, mountaineers must consider the anchor options available, difficulty of movement on the route, and any other objective hazards present. The characteristics of the Soldiers who use the fixed rope are also useful information. Particularly, what their mobility and technical skill levels are and what equipment they have for attaching to the rope. 278 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Intermediate Anchors 11-24. Terrain and vegetation determine the equipment mountaineers need to build the fixed rope. Heavily vegetated terrain or broken rocky terrain may only require cordelettes, slings, and carabiners. Slabby or steep rock faces require cams, nuts, and other lead climbing protection to build anchors. Intermediate anchors must be built robust enough to support the weight of a fall by the number of Soldiers who will move on each section at a given time. When possible, anchors should be built at about waist height in places where good footing is possible so that transitioning past anchors is easier for Soldiers moving on the fixed rope (See figure 11-3 for common methods of attaching ropes to single component anchors.) There should be enough slack to allow Soldiers to follow the easiest path through terrain without adding fall risk. Sometimes a lot of slack is necessary to go around an obstacle or steep section. This is usually better than running a tighter rope over these things, because going around is easier, which reduces the chance of a fall. Other times, a section may need to

Other times, a section may need to be tight to reduce fall distance, such as traversing across a cliff on a narrow ledge. Figure 11-3. Intermediate anchors in moderate terrain, example ATTACHMENT AND MOVEMENT 11-26. The method for movement on fixed ropes with intermediate anchors is as important as how they are constructed. Two primary methods exist for use in steep terrain: the two personal safeties method and the ascender-carabiner method. Choosing between the two is a tradeoff between not carrying heavier single-purpose items and having more security during movement. The two personal safeties method requires no special equipment but cannot eliminate fall risk for a Soldier. The ascender-carabiner method prevents falling but requires each Soldier to carry a piece of equipment that has little other use. Both techniques have their place, and both must be considered for use when planning fixed-rope movements. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 279

Chapter 11 Two Personal Safeties Method 11-27. This method involves having two separate girth hitched slings attached to the tie-in portion of the harness with a single nonlocking carabiner in each. The carabiners are then attached to the fixed rope. Always keep the two carabiners attached to the rope unless they move past an intermediate anchor. To move past an intermediate anchor, clip one carabiner at a time above the anchor. When both carabiners are above the anchor, continue movement. (See figure 11-4.) 11-28. The two personal safeties method is appropriate for situations where the fall consequence is high, but the likelihood is low. It can be used up to 4th-class terrain under good conditions (such as good surface conditions, moderate mobility skills, light loads, well-rested, high visibility) provided that intermediate anchors are appropriately spaced to prevent serious fall injury. Since falls using this method are only stopped by the last anchor a Soldier passed, there is always a chance of injury. This should be considered carefully before choosing it. Figure 11-4. It is preferred when fall risk is substantial or sections of the fixed rope are long, because the ascender captures the Soldiers’ progress as they move. 11-30. To use this technique, girth hitch two slings into the harness. Clip one nonlocking carabiner into one extension. Clip a mechanical ascender to the other extension with a locking carabiner. 11-31. This method is appropriate when both fall consequence and likelihood are high. It can be used in terrain up to 4th class under any conditions. It is the best method when surface conditions are slippery, loads are heavy, mobility skills are low or Soldiers are fatigued, during low visibility, and when intermediate anchors cannot be established to prevent fall injury. Chapter 11 FIXED ROPES IN VERTICAL TERRAIN 11-33. Fixed ropes are sometimes necessary for moving in vertical terrain during complex rescue operations or other special operations in permissive or nontactical environments. They are rarely practical for tactical operations, given their extreme exposure to enemy observation and direct fire. However, vertical terrain is not always avoidable during combat operations, and there are historical examples of their use during pivotal cliff assaults. Vertical terrain is the most extreme example of VDA. Soldiers moving on vertically fixed ropes require well-established overwatch security since they are totally exposed and can do little but ascend the fixed rope. 11-34. Moving on fixed ropes in vertical terrain requires Soldiers to possess the equipment and skills necessary to ascend rope, relying entirely on their attachment to it to prevent fall. Efficient ascending requires specialized equipment. CONSTRUCTING FIXED ROPES IN VERTICAL TERRAIN 11-35. Fixed ropes in vertical terrain are constructed in the same fashion as moderate terrain; however, they take greater technical rope skills, experience with complex anchoring, and time to establish. With fixed ropes in moderate terrain, it would be ideal for the installation team to approach the route from the top and build the system top-down.

they take greater technical rope skills, experience with complex anchoring, and time to establish. With fixed ropes in moderate terrain, it would be ideal for the installation team to approach the route from the top and build the system top-down. However, this is rarely possible. Typically, they must be established from the bottom up by advanced military mountaineers employing lead climbing techniques to get the rope to the top. This process is time-consuming and inherently risky. ASCENDING TECHNIQUES 11-36. Many situations may require a Soldier to ascend a rope in very steep or vertical terrain. Soldiers must be prepared and equipped to do so when operating in 4th- and 5th-class terrain. Typically, ascending rope is a more efficient technique than climbing for moving followers over hard climbing terrain, to include those members of small assault climber teams. 11-37. The techniques described below are for single strands of rope, so it is imperative that appropriate measures are taken to pad the rope near sharp edges. Whenever Soldiers plan to ascend vertical terrain, they should use mechanical ascenders to achieve maximum safety and efficiency during movement. 11-38. Ascending techniques are also key skills used in rescue operations, self-rescue during crevasse fall, and

rope near sharp edges. Whenever Soldiers plan to ascend vertical terrain, they should use mechanical ascenders to achieve maximum safety and efficiency during movement. 11-38. Ascending techniques are also key skills used in rescue operations, self-rescue during crevasse fall, and whenever rappellers find their rope does not reach the ground. Prusik Ascent 11-39. Two prusiks can be used to ascend rope. One prusik is tied to the fixed rope using a cordelette at approximately forehead height. A fixed loop is tied in the hanging tails to create an attachment point at about waist level. This is then secured to the harness with a locking carabiner. Another prusik is tied to the fixed rope at about waist level. The hanging tails are then tied to one or both feet using any appropriate knot to form a foot stirrup. (See figure 11-6.) 11-40. The upper prusik serves as the “progress capture,” during ascent, by holding the Soldier up, while the lower friction hitch serves as the “progress” or makeshift foothold. During movement, the lower hitch is slid up as high as possible while hanging from the upper hitch. Soldiers then stand up on the lower hitch, pushing down and behind them with

hitch serves as the “progress” or makeshift foothold. During movement, the lower hitch is slid up as high as possible while hanging from the upper hitch. Soldiers then stand up on the lower hitch, pushing down and behind them with their leg, while sliding the upper hitch as high as possible. They then rest in the harness from the upper hitch and continue. Safety knots should be tied in the fixed rope below the lower hitch and attached to the harness with a locking carabiner every 10 to 15 feet. This provides a backup against failure of the friction hitch to grab. This technique should be considered an improvised technique for use when ascending is not expected. 282 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Figure 11-6. Prusik ascent Prusik Ascender Method 11-41. Mechanical ascenders are a one-directional device used to capture progress along a rope and assist climbers as they ascend steep, vertical, or free-hanging terrain. They can be substituted for one or both hitches described in prusik ascent. They make ascending efficient and fast. 11-42. To use an ascender as a progress capture, attach it to the rope at about head height. Girth hitch a sling or cordelette to the harness, and then use a locking carabiner to secure the other end to the bottom of the ascender, forming an arm-length extension between them. Commonly, a nonlocking carabiner is clipped around the rope through the top of the ascender for added security. This prevents the device from twisting off the rope. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 283

Chapter 11 11-43. To create the progress with an ascender, attach it to the rope at about waist height. Girth hitch or use any carabiner to attach a sling or cordelette to the bottom of the carabiner and tie it to one or both feet using any appropriate knot. The movement process is the same as described above for prusik ascent. 11-44. There are dozens of devices available that work the same as an ascender. Ensure the rope type and diameter are appropriate for the device used, as most mechanical devices have a specified range of acceptable use. Read all manufacturers’ instructions to ensure safe use. 11-45. Stopper knots should be tied in the fixed rope below the lower hitch or device and attached to the harness with a locking carabiner every 10 to 15 feet. This provides a backup against the rope grabs slipping. This technique should be used when ascending is planned but not enough ascenders are available for Soldiers to be issued two. Double-Ascender Method 11-46. This technique is extremely efficient once it has been practiced. It is a recommended technique for ascending long distances. An etrier or cordelette forming a foot stirrup is hung off each

for Soldiers to be issued two. Double-Ascender Method 11-46. This technique is extremely efficient once it has been practiced. It is a recommended technique for ascending long distances. An etrier or cordelette forming a foot stirrup is hung off each ascender with a locking carabiner. Both ascenders are then placed on the rope. A cordelette or sling also hangs off each ascender and is girth hitched to the user’s harness, creating two attachment points to the rope. (See figure 11-7.) 11-47. To use the system, the Soldier places a foot in each etrier (or stirrup) and slides the upper ascender up the rope. This upper ascender is easier to move because the Soldier’s weight is on the lower ascender. The lower ascender is moved up next, while the upper ascender supports the Soldier’s weight. Sometimes it is necessary to slightly release the camming mechanism before moving an ascender. 11-48. It is also recommended to tie back-up knots periodically in the same manner as prusik ascent. 11-49. This technique is the most efficient and is recommended for use whenever ascending is a planned movement technique. 284 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Figure 11-7. Double-ascender ascent SPECIAL TECHNIQUES AND CONSIDERATIONS 11-50. There are too many considerations for using and improving fixed ropes to cover them all in this training circular. However, the following techniques should be considered for use with fixed ropes. Weapon Management 11-51. Unless enemy attack is imminent, weapons should be slung to the rear, allowing Soldiers to scramble more easily in difficult terrain. Heavier weapons, such as sniper weapon systems, mortars, and machine guns, may need to be attached to the top of rucksacks. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 285

Chapter 11 Improving Steps 11-52. Soldiers are less likely to fall and move more quickly if they have good footing. Hard snow is especially easy to carve steps into and can allow Soldiers to move with less exertion on their calf muscles. Carving steps should be done first in steeper sections and, as time allows, in other areas too. Platforms can also be made where Soldiers are transitioning past intermediate anchors. If a Soldier can easily stand near an intermediate anchor, they can clip around it much faster. This greatly lessens the time required for the group to navigate terrain where objective hazards may be present. Etriers or Slings at Difficult Steps 11-53. The hanging of a sling or etrier (for use as a hand or foothold) where there is a difficult step can help reduce fall potential and increase speed of the group. An etrier is a short ladder that can be made from any piece of rope or cord and creates an artificial step in a place where there is no natural feature to step on. The etrier can be hung off an intermediate anchor or its own anchor. (See figure 11-8.) Caving Ladders 11-54. Manufactured ladders can

cord and creates an artificial step in a place where there is no natural feature to step on. The etrier can be hung off an intermediate anchor or its own anchor. (See figure 11-8.) Caving Ladders 11-54. Manufactured ladders can be useful for large steps and crevasse negotiation. They also enable Soldiers to navigate challenging terrain in the dark, much easier than if they had to search for hand and foot placements. Some are constructed of materials that can be rolled up for transport. While they may make the ascent of a blank wall easier, they are cumbersome to carry. Cables and Via-Ferrata 11-55. If terrain is to be repetitively used for access to higher points for something semi-permanent such as an observation post, it may be in the unit’s best interest to build a via-ferrata style system for access. A via-ferrata works similarly to a fixed rope with intermediate anchors, except it uses cable instead of rope. Using cable reduces the need for constant inspection and greatly increases durability. They are much more time consuming to build, but it may be the most feasible option if a unit uses a piece of terrain for an extended period. Given the

reduces the need for constant inspection and greatly increases durability. They are much more time consuming to build, but it may be the most feasible option if a unit uses a piece of terrain for an extended period. Given the cable’s rigidity, the attachment method used by Soldiers needs to provide the stretch to lessen fall forces. This equipment can be found on the civilian market. Another component of a via-ferrata-style system is the addition of metal ladder style and foot and handholds. These are for areas and routes that will see traffic over a long time, making the use of soft materials impractical. 286 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Figure 11-8. Etrier styles SECTION II – TYPES OF RAPPELLING 11-56. Rappelling is a method of descending steep terrain using a rope and a means of creating friction to control the rate of descent. This provides Soldiers with a safe way to descend terrain that would otherwise expose them to very high fall risks. 11-57. If the descent distance is greater than a rope length (for example, multipitch), multiple, simple fixed lines can be linked together with anchors at the top and bottom of each rope. Soldiers can then rappel from anchor to anchor and transition from rope to rope until they reach the ground. This method requires many resources and numerous personnel to establish and manage safely. 11-58. Small teams with fewer resources must use the one or two ropes they can carry to rappel the whole group from one anchor to a lower one, then retrieve the rope, and repeat the process until the ground is reached. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 287

Chapter 11 RAPPELLING FUNDAMENTALS 11-59. Rappelling is a quick method of descent, but it can be extremely dangerous. The dangers include anchor failure, equipment failure, and individual error. Carefully select anchors in a mountainous environment. In a mountain environment, take great care to load the anchor slowly and to ensure that no excessive stress is placed on the anchor. To ensure this, prohibit bounding while rappelling; Soldiers should slowly descend. Soldiers should avoid dragging their feet when moving backwards towards the edge as this causes rockfall. 11-60. Soldiers rappelling with weapons should sling them on the back or to the side when wearing packs. Soldiers carrying particularly heavy weapons, such as machine guns, sniper rifles, or mortars may need to strap them to the top of their pack and use additional techniques described below to make rappelling less difficult. RAPPEL SITE SELECTION 11-61. Selecting the rappel point depends on factors, such as mission, cover, route, anchor availability, and edge composition (for example, avoiding those with loose or jagged rocks). The anchor selected should leave no doubt that it will work for its intended purpose. 11-62. Rappel ropes anchored at waist level or above make transitioning over the edge much easier

(for example, avoiding those with loose or jagged rocks). The anchor selected should leave no doubt that it will work for its intended purpose. 11-62. Rappel ropes anchored at waist level or above make transitioning over the edge much easier and reduce the likelihood of Soldiers stumbling or falling. Stumbles and falls are likely to increase the risk of rope damage on sharp rock as well as increase force exerted on anchors. 11-63. Rappel sites with suitable loading and off-loading platforms should be selected. Ideally, they are flat and allow for anchoring far enough away from the edge that Soldiers do not need to be attached to an anchor to prevent accidentally falling off the edge. If this is impossible, use fixed-rope techniques described in section I when approaching the rappel point. A staging area large enough to hold the group in a safe place nearby is also desirable. INSTALLATION CONSIDERATIONS 11-64. The two major factors in deciding how to attach a rappel rope to an anchor are whether the rope needs to be retrievable from the bottom and whether redundancy in rappel rope strands is necessary for safety. Both characteristics cannot be achieved at the same time. 11-65. In

attach a rappel rope to an anchor are whether the rope needs to be retrievable from the bottom and whether redundancy in rappel rope strands is necessary for safety. Both characteristics cannot be achieved at the same time. 11-65. In an operational environment, or during advanced military mountaineering training, ropes must be retrievable. This is because there is presumably no other feasible way to negotiate the vertical obstacle, or the group would be using it. All people and equipment must rappel, and the rope must be recovered for future use. This means that the rope cannot be fixed to the top anchor when the last Soldier begins rappelling. 11-66. When training basic rappelling, retrieving ropes is not necessary. Appropriate rappel sites for inexperienced rappellers should include access between the top and bottom by some other safe means for set up and breakdown. This allows for a greater safety margin by using two fixed independent strands for rappel ropes. Not only does this add redundancy to the system, but also using two strands replicates typical rappelling in an operational environment. 11-67. Anchors that support the maximum force rappellers could exert should be established as described in chapter 9. All rigging should

does this add redundancy to the system, but also using two strands replicates typical rappelling in an operational environment. 11-67. Anchors that support the maximum force rappellers could exert should be established as described in chapter 9. All rigging should be inspected by a qualified advanced military mountaineer, at a minimum. RETRIEVABLE RAPPELS 11-68. Retrievable rappels can be established using appropriate single-point anchors (such as a tree, boulder, horn of rock) using only the rope, or they can be attached to cordelettes, or webbing tied around the anchor feature. If other materials are used, then they cannot be retrieved from the bottom. 11-69. Multipoint anchors require additional materials to establish. This material cannot be retrieved from the bottom. 11-70. The minimum necessary equipment should be used in building retrievable rappel anchors. 288 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Half-Rope Length 11-71. The simplest and most common method is to just run one end of the rope around anchor feature, and then double back stack it until the middle of the rope is around the anchor feature. This ensures both strands are the same length. Tie a stopper knot at the bottom end with both strands leaving 12- to 18-inch tails. This prevents accidentally rappelling off the end of the rope. The ropes are then thrown or back stacked over the edge. 11-72. Sometimes the rope cannot be routed directly around the anchor. The rope can then be back stacked so that the middle of the rope passes through the attachment point for an anchor made from cordelette or webbing or clipped to it using a locking carabiner. 11-73. If a rope could be cut, it is possible to make the system redundant for all but the last rappeller. This system is established in the same manner as above, but once complete a BHK is tied close to the anchor with both strands. This creates two fixed independent strands and adds redundancy to the system. Before the last Soldiers begin to rappel, they simply untie the BHK,

as above, but once complete a BHK is tied close to the anchor with both strands. This creates two fixed independent strands and adds redundancy to the system. Before the last Soldiers begin to rappel, they simply untie the BHK, and the system is retrievable again. Full-Length Rope 11-74. Full-length rappels require two standard-length ropes. Route the end of one rope around or through the anchor point and tie a flat double overhand with the ends of both ropes joining them. Double back stack the ropes and tie a stopper knot as described above. Using a flat overhand to join the rappel ropes reduces the likelihood of the knot being stuck in vegetation of rock features during retrieval. 11-75. Full-length rappels can be made redundant for all but the last rappeller in the same manner as is described above. Rappel Rope Retrieval 11-76. Once all Soldiers have reached the bottom and any stopper knots have been untied, the rope can be retrieved by pulling one strand. The other strand travels up to the anchor and falls. If there are any knots in it, they can become jammed in the anchor and prevent rope retrieval. It is a good idea to

be retrieved by pulling one strand. The other strand travels up to the anchor and falls. If there are any knots in it, they can become jammed in the anchor and prevent rope retrieval. It is a good idea to get excess personnel away from the area prior to pulling in case any loose rocks are dislodged above. 11-77. When pulling the rope on a multipitch rappel, it is a good idea to route the end being pulled through the next anchor, so the rope is less likely to be dropped. RAPPELS WITH FIXED STRANDS 11-78. Whenever a threat of the installation rope being cut is identified, two fixed independent strands should be used. Two strands add redundancy and reduce the likelihood that a fall may occur in a cut rope incident. Installations with two fixed independent strands are typically the standard for rappelling training whether a hazard has been identified. Half-Rope Length 11-79. If using a single anchor, anchor the middle of the rope to it with a bowline knot. If using a preequalized multipoint anchor, tie a fixed loop in the middle of the rope, and attach it to the anchor with two opposing locking carabiners. Full-Rope Length

the middle of the rope to it with a bowline knot. If using a preequalized multipoint anchor, tie a fixed loop in the middle of the rope, and attach it to the anchor with two opposing locking carabiners. Full-Rope Length 11-80. Anchor the rappel ropes by tying a bowline knot with the top ends of both ropes. 11-81. Situations may arise where the distance of anchors from each other, or the distance of the anchors from the rappel point, requires using a second rope to construct an anchor, or extend the anchor master point closer to the loading platform, allowing for the maximum amount of rope to be utilized for the rappel. In this case, tie a fixed loop with the top ends of both ropes, and clip it to the anchor system master point using two opposing locking carabiners. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 289

Chapter 11 RAPPEL INSTALLATION SPECIAL TECHNIQUES 11-82. There are a few problems that mountaineers should be prepared to solve related to rappelling. The common problems are damaged ropes, short ropes, and the threat of a rope being cut when retrievability is necessary. Damaged Rope 11-83. Ropes occasionally become damaged but may need to be used until they can be replaced following an operation. Mountaineers must be familiar with how to safely use damaged ropes for rappelling. 11-84. First, tie an overhand knot, isolating the damaged spot in the rope. The rope can then continue to be used for many mountaineering tasks. However, the knot in the rope prevents Soldiers from rappelling past. 11-85. If a retrievable rappel is necessary, the damaged rope can be used as follows. The rope is back stacked around the anchor as usual. A fixed bight is tied in the damaged strand near the anchor. That bight is then clipped to the nondamaged strand with a locking carabiner. When loaded, the carabiner fits snug to the anchor like a slip knot. (See figure 11-9.) Both strands of rope are thrown or back stacked off the cliff. 11-86. Soldiers can then rig for rappel using only the

locking carabiner. When loaded, the carabiner fits snug to the anchor like a slip knot. (See figure 11-9.) Both strands of rope are thrown or back stacked off the cliff. 11-86. Soldiers can then rig for rappel using only the nondamaged strand and descend the obstacle. Note. Rappelling on a single strand creates less friction. 11-87. Once all Soldiers have rappelled, the damaged strand, or tagline, can be pulled to retrieve the rope. The nondamaged strand travels up through the carabiner, around the anchor and back down. More care should be taken when pulling the rope because it is more likely to become hung up using this technique. This technique also works when a full-length rappel is necessary and one of the ropes is damaged near the middle. Figure 11-9. Tagline retrievable rappel using a tagline 290 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Short Rope 11-88. Sometimes a group may only have one rope that is not long enough to reach the bottom of a cliff, and the rope cannot be retrieved because the cliff is taller than a half-rope length. 11-89. If the group has enough cordelettes or shorter sections of rope, it can solve the problem. To do so, one end of the rope is lowered until it is on the ground. Cordelettes are then joined by a single strand to the other end until they reach the ground. 11-90. The installation is then rigged to be retrievable with a tagline (as described in paragraphs 11-83 through 11-87, page 290). Soldiers can then rappel on the strand of static rope. When personnel are at the bottom, the end with the cordelettes can be pulled to retrieve the rope. Take more care when pulling the rope because it is more likely to become hung up using this technique. 11-91. Small units can use this technique to reduce the weight of rope they need to carry. Rather than carry two full-sized ropes to rappel a full-rope length, they can carry one rope and a 6- or 7-mm tagline that is cut

units can use this technique to reduce the weight of rope they need to carry. Rather than carry two full-sized ropes to rappel a full-rope length, they can carry one rope and a 6- or 7-mm tagline that is cut the same length from a spool, or plan to use joined cordelettes that are spread out amongst their members. Threat of Cut Rope Using a Retrievable System 11-92. Some situations may require a retrievable rappel, but a threat to the rope is identified (such as sharp rock or falling rock hazard) that cannot be mitigated by simply padding an edge. This problem can be resolved by one of two methods. 11-93. The first involves establishing the retrievable rappel system described above, and then attaching a tube-style device and locking carabiner tight to the anchor. This effectively fixes both strands. All but the last Soldier conducts the rappel with fixed strands. The last Soldier uses the attached device and rappels carefully as normal. This limits the exposure of all but one Soldier to the threat of cut rope. The rope can be pulled from below as previously described. 11-94. The second involves establishing the retrievable rappel system described above, and then

as normal. This limits the exposure of all but one Soldier to the threat of cut rope. The rope can be pulled from below as previously described. 11-94. The second involves establishing the retrievable rappel system described above, and then tying a big knot close to the anchor with both strands fixing them. All but the last Soldier conducts the rappel with fixed strands. The last Soldier unties the knot and rappels carefully as normal. This limits the exposure of all but one Soldier to the threat of cut rope. The rope can be pulled from below as previously described. RAPPELLING TECHNIQUES 11-95. Different situations call for different rappel attachment techniques. They vary in how much friction they produce, the security in which the rappeller is attached to the rope, and whether they allow the rappeller to go hands free. The consequence of falling determines the type of attachment to the rope. Terrain severity determines how much friction is required to control descent. Whether or not other tasks need to be conducted mid-rappel determines the need for a hands-free brake. 11-96. During rappelling, the body generally forms an L-shape with the feet shoulder-width apart, legs straight, and buttocks parallel to

to control descent. Whether or not other tasks need to be conducted mid-rappel determines the need for a hands-free brake. 11-96. During rappelling, the body generally forms an L-shape with the feet shoulder-width apart, legs straight, and buttocks parallel to the ground. When carrying equipment or additional weight, a modified L-shape is used with the legs slightly lower than the buttocks to compensate for the additional weight. The rappeller’s back is straight. Rappellers never let go of the ropes with their brake hand until the rappel is complete. Rappellers should keep their feet flat against the surface they are rappelling down and their weight fully on the rope throughout the rappel. Hasty Rappel 11-97. The hasty rappel technique is only used on low-angle slopes. Its primary advantages are that it is simple to learn and execute and requires no specialized equipment. However, take care not to underestimate the terrain being negotiated. Application of this technique in terrain that is too steep can have deadly consequences. The level of rappeller surefootedness determines the severity of terrain for which this technique is appropriate. Gloves can be worn to prevent rope burns. 11-98. Facing slightly sideways to the anchor, rappellers place the ropes

steep can have deadly consequences. The level of rappeller surefootedness determines the severity of terrain for which this technique is appropriate. Gloves can be worn to prevent rope burns. 11-98. Facing slightly sideways to the anchor, rappellers place the ropes horizontally across their back, under their armpits, and palm up. The hand nearest to the anchor is the guide hand, and the other is the brake hand. Bending the rope around the body increases friction. (See figure 11-10, page 292.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 291

Chapter 11 11-99. While moving, Soldiers should keep their legs as perpendicular to the slope as possible, leaning into the rope. This increases the security of foot placements and reduces the likelihood of a slip and fall. 11-100. To stop, rappellers rotate their body to face uphill and bring their brake hand across the front of their body to their opposite shoulder. Figure 11-10. Hasty rappel Munter Hitch Rappel 11-101. This method provides adequate friction and control and is the simplest and easiest method of rappelling to establish on steep terrain when without a standard rappel device. Most often, it is used as a backup for when a more efficient device is lost or forgotten. 11-102. The drawback of using a Munter hitch is that it twists the rope, causing snarl at the bottom that makes future use difficult. An experienced Soldier can separate the strands with the brake hand and counter the twist of the rope as it feeds through the hitch to lessen this effect. It is not recommended to have multiple Soldiers rappel on the same rope using this method. Twisting is lessened if the rappel is on steep terrain and the strands 292 TC 3-97.61 26

Fixed Ropes do not touch the ground. This allows the twists to undo themselves. Twisting becomes more of a problem if the terrain is at a low angle, and the rope is mostly lying on the ground. 11-103. To use this technique, attach a locking carabiner into a harness. Then tie a Munter hitch in both strands of the rappel rope and place it in the locking carabiner. (See figure 11-11.) 11-104. Descent is controlled in the same way as with the devices described above. Figure 11-11. Munter hitch rappel Figure-Eight Descender 11-105. Using a figure-eight descender provides a secure attachment to the rappel rope and adequate friction for use in steep-to-vertical terrain. 11-106. The advantage of these is that they work well with both larger diameter ropes and static or low-stretch ropes. The disadvantages are that they are less versatile, heavier, and bulkier than tube-style devices, which serve multiple mountaineering purposes. 11-107. To rig the device for descent, pass a double bight through the large opening, and then around the smaller one. Then attach the figure eight to a harness using a locking carabiner through the small opening. (See figure 11-12, page 294.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 293

Chapter 11 11-108. Soldiers assume a typical L-shaped position while rappelling and control their rate of descent with the brake strand by slowly feeding slack from below them toward the device. Two hands should be used on the brake strand, positioned in front of the body below the device. Figure 11-12. Figure-eight descender Tube-Style Devices 11-109. Using a tube-style device provides a secure attachment to the rappel rope and adequate friction for use in steep to vertical terrain. 11-110. Most climbing teams use these. The advantages are that they can be used for both belaying and rappelling with one or two ropes. They are compact and lightweight. They do not twist the ropes as much as figure-eight descenders. The disadvantages are that they do not work as smoothly when used with static or low-stretch ropes due to the more tightly woven rope sheath and stiffer feel. They also do not typically work well on ropes larger than 11 mm in diameter. 294 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes 11-111. To rig the device for descent, pinch the rappel rope into a double bight, and then pass one through each hole in the tube starting on the side without a wire hanger. Clip a locking carabiner through the wire hanger and both bights of rope. Then attach the device to a harness with a locking carabiner so that the brake strands are oriented down or toward the intended brake hand. (See figure 11-13.) 11-112. Descent is controlled in the same way as with figure-eight descenders. Figure 11-13. Rappelling with a tube-style device Extending Rappel Devices 11-113. Using an extension moves the rappel device away from the body. This makes it easier to keep two hands on the brake strands. It also reduces the chance of straps or clothing from being caught in the device and stopping rope from feeding through it. This results in the rappeller becoming stuck on the rope, unable to descend, and requires advanced skills to fix. Wearing bulky cold-weather clothing or tactical load-bearing harnesses increase the likelihood of this occurring. Extending the device allows for the use of a hands-free backup. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 295

Chapter 11 11-114. To extend a device, create an extension by girth hitching a sling to the harness. Insert the rappel ropes into the device as described above and clip them into the extension with a locking carabiner. A basket hitch can also be used to create a shorter extension. Under most circumstances, it is recommended to use an extension when rappelling in mountainous terrain because it makes controlling descent easier and less fatiguing to the core when heavy loads are carried. Rappels using the Munter hitch technique cannot be extended. Hands-Free Backup 11-115. A hands-free backup is a rigging technique, involving friction hitches or mechanical devices that prevent a load from falling should control of a brake strand be lost. To establish a hands-free backup, tie an autoblock around the rappel ropes below the device, and attach it to the climber’s harness with a locking carabiner. (See figure 11-15, page 300.) Any time an autoblock is used, it must be tested to ensure it grabs before starting the rappel. If it does not, more wraps should be added until it does. 11-116. This allows Soldiers to perform other tasks mid-rappel. The most common example is the first rappeller needing

be tested to ensure it grabs before starting the rappel. If it does not, more wraps should be added until it does. 11-116. This allows Soldiers to perform other tasks mid-rappel. The most common example is the first rappeller needing to untangle the rope on the way down. During rappelling, Soldiers must prevent the autoblock from engaging and stopping their downward progress with one hand while the other feeds rope to the device. To engage the autoblock, the Soldier ceases minding the autoblock and it will engage, forcing the rappel rope into the brake position. When Soldiers are ready to continue rappelling, they resume control of the brake strands with both hands and disengage the autoblock. Descent can then continue. 11-117. Chapter 12 Hauling and Lowering Techniques Mountain warfare requires moving Soldiers, weapons, and equipment up, over, and down steep, rugged terrain. It is vital that Soldiers understand the principles and fundamental concepts of hauling and lowering heavy loads both efficiently and safely. SECTION I – HAULING TECHNIQUES 12-1. Mountain operations involve many situations that require hauling systems. A hauling system is a technical rope system used to move a load up steep or vertical terrain comprised of rigging that generates increased mechanical advantage (MA) and captures progress. Properly using hauling systems allows Soldiers to move heavy loads through terrain obstacles that would have been impossible to overcome otherwise. Common situations requiring these systems are equipment recovery, resupply, and rescue operations. Choosing the right system for a given situation requires understanding the principles of MA, categories of systems, and solid judgement. MECHANICAL ADVANTAGE 12-2. A mechanical advantage is a reduction in the force required to move a load, which comes at the cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage. During hauling operations, MA can be created using a rope through several rigging techniques. The advantage gained reduces the amount of force that is necessary

the cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage. During hauling operations, MA can be created using a rope through several rigging techniques. The advantage gained reduces the amount of force that is necessary to move a load vertically. This makes hauling heavy loads easier. When choosing and constructing a hauling system, the goal is to use the lowest level of MA to move the load. As MA increases, efficiency and load sensitivity decrease. Efficiency is lost throughout the system anytime the rope touches a surface (including the edge of the cliff), moves through carabiners or pulleys, and rubs on itself in the system. Load sensitivity is the ability of the Soldier pulling on the rope to feel what is happening to the load on the end of the rope. For example, a Soldier pulling a heavy load up a slope by hand will know immediately if the load becomes stuck on an obstacle. However, a Soldier moving the load using a high level of MA would not feel this until there was a large amount of tension in the system. This is important when moving casualties or sensitive equipment. These systems require time,

However, a Soldier moving the load using a high level of MA would not feel this until there was a large amount of tension in the system. This is important when moving casualties or sensitive equipment. These systems require time, materials, and personnel to construct and operate. The intent is not to make easy work of moving the load. The lowest level of MA is desired to maximize load sensitivity, efficiency, and time. 12-3. The more MA a rope system produces, the less efficient it will be. For example, a Soldier operating a 5:1 system only needs to exert 1/5 of the pulling force to move the load. However, that Soldier will need to pull 5 feet of rope through the system for the load to move 1 foot. A balance between work and efficiency must be achieved when selecting an appropriate MA for a given situation. HAULING SYSTEM COMPONENTS 12-4. The hauling system has five basic components. Understanding how they work to move the load together (see the list below) allows Soldiers to achieve greater efficiency during hauling: • Anchors—the anchors required for hauling a heavy load must be unquestionable (see chapter 9). Anchors should be located away from

TECHNIQUES TO REDUCE FRICTION 12-13. Friction reduces efficiency of rope movement and can drastically reduce MA. It is important to identify points of friction within the system and strive to reduce them. Efficiency is lost throughout the system anytime the rope touches hardware. Friction can be minimized by using pulleys. Pulleys are used to change direction in rope systems. Pulleys should be small, lightweight, and rated for mountaineering applications. They should accommodate the largest diameter of rope being used. Pulleys are made with several bearings, different-sized sheaves (wheels), and metal alloy side plates. (See figure 12-8, page 310.) Always avoid plastic pulleys. The side plate should rotate on the pulley axle to allow the pulley to be attached at any point along the rope. For best results, the sheave diameter must be at least four times larger than

Always avoid plastic pulleys. The side plate should rotate on the pulley axle to allow the pulley to be attached at any point along the rope. For best results, the sheave diameter must be at least four times larger than the rope’s diameter to maintain high rope strength. Pulleys with side plates designed to accommodate prusik knots are referred to as prusik minding pulleys. These pulleys are designed with tolerances that allow the ropes to run through them but block the passage of a prusik hitch, preventing it from being caught in the pulley. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 309

The difference between a system that uses pulleys at direction changes and the same system that only uses carabiners is significant. If the team only has a few pulleys, they should be used at the direction changes closest to the system’s haul strand. Pulleys in these locations will maximize the force put into the system initially and carry 90-percent efficiency farther through the system. 12-15. Friction also occurs where the mainline contacts the edge of the slope or cliff. If a suitable anchor can be found near the edge, this friction point can be minimized. The mainline can be lifted and routed through a high directional at the top of the slope or cliff to reduce rope contact and friction at the edge. (See figure 12-9.) 310 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025
