A lowering system is a technical rope system used to move a load down steep or vertical terrain in a controlled fashion using friction hitches or mechanical devices. These sorts of systems are used to control the speed of descent for personnel or equipment using rope. They are an integral part of both highand low-angle rescue. (See chapter 15.) Lowering a victim or a load is always preferred over hauling if the terrain and situation allows. No two situations are identical. Each new situation will dictate which lowering techniques and systems are appropriate. Understanding basic lowering concepts is key to achieving a safe and efficient solution to the problem. The bottom line for any lowering system is that enough friction must be created to safely control the descent of the load. Different terrain demands different methods of creating friction. Chapter 13 Mountain Stream Crossing In 480 BC, Persian King Xerxes constructed a pontoon bridge that spanned a mile and a quarter across the Hellespont. After a previous failure to take Greece, the king weighed the options of either finding alternate routes to the north that added months to his expedition or pinpoint potential water crossing locations for his army. Xerxes insisted on the fastest and most direct route across the Aegean inlet for his 300,000 men. While negotiating the linear obstacle involved massive resources and engineering, it would save precious time for his army to reach their objective. SECTION I – MOUNTAIN STREAM FUNDAMENTALS 13-1. A mountain stream crossing is essentially an approach to negotiating a potentially swift and cold waterway that Soldiers may encounter in the mountains. Learning to cross small streams forms a foundation of skills for personnel to manage larger streams and rivers, where consequences could be far more hazardous. 13-2. In an operation involving the crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to protect remaining personnel. This operation

crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to protect remaining personnel. This operation should be conducted economically and with minimal loss of momentum. 13-3. There are limits on the safe use of the techniques discussed in this chapter. Not all mountain rivers or streams will be fordable with these techniques. If a water obstacle is too wide, swift, or deep, an alternate route should be used. It may require using aircraft transport if engineer support is unavailable. Reconnaissance of questionable crossing sites is essential. This chapter covers the techniques for crossing mountain streams that have a depth generally not exceeding waist level. 13-4. Stream crossings should not be taken lightly. The force of flowing water may be extremely great and is most often underestimated. All rivers and streams are obstacles to movement. They should be treated as danger areas and avoided whenever possible. When rivers or streams must be crossed, there are many techniques that the small-unit leader may choose from, depending upon the type of stream, its width, speed of the current,

should be treated as danger areas and avoided whenever possible. When rivers or streams must be crossed, there are many techniques that the small-unit leader may choose from, depending upon the type of stream, its width, speed of the current, and depth of the water. This activity should be rehearsed prior to execution in the operational environment. RECONNAISSANCE 13-5. Performing a site survey of potential crossing locations (map, photo, or aerial) may not always reveal that a water obstacle exists. In a swamp, for example, unfordable sloughs may not show on the map, and they may be concealed from aerial observation by a canopy of vegetation. 13-6. Site selection is extremely important once Soldiers determine that they must make a crossing. Elevated positions offer an optimal vantage point from which to analyze a large area of possibilities. This is sometimes better than a hundred close views from a riverbank. Select the site selection before the main body arrives and examine the site around a similar time of day that the crossing will be conducted. 13-7. A suitable crossing site should have specific characteristics. A river crossing site should limit exposure to observation, facilitate the installation team crossing (if necessary) or

the site around a similar time of day that the crossing will be conducted. 13-7. A suitable crossing site should have specific characteristics. A river crossing site should limit exposure to observation, facilitate the installation team crossing (if necessary) or swimming with ropes, and minimize drowning hazards. Care must be taken to avoid an installation team crossing upstream of rapids, waterfalls, or fallen trees in the river. For dry features, such as gorges or ravines, the site should facilitate the installation team’s descent and ascent crossing while minimizing any falling hazards that exist. While dry crossings are preferred to wet crossings for speed and safety factors, they can become locations for an enemy to place landmines and improvised explosive devices. 13-8. The time of day is an important factor. Recent precipitation or increased temperatures could cause water levels to rise as glaciers or snow-covered peaks begin to melt. Early morning crossings are preferred, as the cooler night temperatures usually reduce the melt from snow and ice. A morning crossing also allows clothing items to dry throughout the day. Whether a crossing is made in daylight or in darkness depends on 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 323

A crossing point should be chosen where the river widens. The sudden width of the channel normally yields a shallow depth. Avoid sharp turns in the river or a narrowing choke point in the river or stream since the water is likely to be deep and have a strong current on the outside of the bend for curves. 13-10. Many mountain streams, especially those fed by glacier runoff, contain sections with numerous braided channels. While often shallower than a main river, this changing landscape offers little in the way of cover and concealment of exposed personnel. Shoals, or partially submerged sandbars, can act like quicksand depending on the riverbed composition. 13-11. Riverbanks should be low enough to accommodate for easy entry and exit from the water. Banks that are tall and steep may require employing installations such as hasty rappels (see figure 11-11, page 293) or simple fixed ropes (see figure 11-2, page 278). 13-12. Chapter 14 Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue Ten percent of the Earth’s land mass is covered by glaciers. Glaciers are rivers of ice flowing under the influence of gravity, constantly restructuring the mountains around them. They often provide the best route in otherwise impassable terrain but can contain crevasses and other hazards that can cause injury, death, or compromise a unit’s mission. Soldiers operating in glaciated terrain must understand these hazards, be well versed in the fundamentals of glacier travel, and be proficient with crevasse rescue techniques. SECTION I – GLACIER FUNDAMENTALS 14-1. Glaciers can be large enough to cover an entire continent. They may move only inches or hundreds of feet a year. Movement is caused by gravity, slippage over the bedrock, or by the internal flow in the ice. It is important for route planning and risk management to understand glacial features and understand how they form and move. Dismounted movement across glaciers is hazardous; however, glaciers often provide the easiest passage through more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces. GLACIERS 14-2. Glaciers form over time by the weight of accumulating snow compressing older layers of snow into ice. As snow accumulates, gravity takes over and the

provide the easiest passage through more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces. GLACIERS 14-2. Glaciers form over time by the weight of accumulating snow compressing older layers of snow into ice. As snow accumulates, gravity takes over and the ice begins to move downhill. The weight of millions of pounds of ice makes a small film of water that acts as a lubricant, enabling it to slide. 14-3. The upper part of the glacier where the annual snow accumulation exceeds the melt is called the accumulation zone. Further down the glacier, the area where melt exceeds accumulation is an area called the ablation zone. The imaginary line between the two zones is known as the firn line. CLASSIFICATION 14-4. There are two classifications of glaciers: alpine glaciers and ice caps. Alpine glaciers form in high mountain bowls. Ice caps can cover thousands of square miles, such as those that cover Greenland and Antarctica. TYPES OF ALPINE GLACIERS 14-5. The following are four types of glaciers: • Valley glacier—resides and flows in a valley. • Cirque glacier—forms and resides in a bowl. These do not advance beyond the bowl. • Hanging glacier—these are a result of valley or cirque glaciers

following are four types of glaciers: • Valley glacier—resides and flows in a valley. • Cirque glacier—forms and resides in a bowl. These do not advance beyond the bowl. • Hanging glacier—these are a result of valley or cirque glaciers flowing and deteriorating. As the movement continues, portions separate and are sometimes left hanging on mountains, ridgelines, or cliffs. • Piedmont glacier—formed by one or more valley glaciers, spreads out into a large area. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 333

Chapter 14 GLACIER OBSTACLES 14-6. Units intending to use glaciers for travel routes must be familiar with their hazards and characteristics to ensure safe and efficient movement on them. Failure to identify and prepare for obstacles, which can come in the form of vertical terrain, can slow or prevent movement. Failure to identify and prepare for hazards can result in significant injury or loss of life. 14-7. Glaciers contain many different features that can impede travel. (See figure 14-1.) They are— • Bergschrund—the bergschrund is a giant crevasse found at the upper limit of glacier movement. It is formed where the moving glacier breaks away from the ice cap or snowfield above. The bergschrund can be high and overhanging and can create an obstacle to movement when moving from the valley floor onto the mountainsides. • Crevasses—crevasses are cracks in the glacier caused by irregularities in the bedrock under the glacier as it moves and flows. Crevasses often form where the angle of the slope increases greatly, causing tension to split open the snow and ice. They also commonly form wherever the glacier makes a turn. They can be transverse, longitudinal, or lateral, depending on their orientation to the direction

the angle of the slope increases greatly, causing tension to split open the snow and ice. They also commonly form wherever the glacier makes a turn. They can be transverse, longitudinal, or lateral, depending on their orientation to the direction of the glacier’s movement. Crevasses can be 200-feet deep but are normally 40- to 100-feet deep. Crevasses often hinder travel across glaciers. Snow often conceals crevasses, causing possible major falling hazards to Soldiers. Bypassing them can increase travel time and distance. Snow bridges that form over them can give way without warning. During the summer, the ice is less covered with snow and most crevasses are exposed. They can still be hazardous at night or in reduced visibility. • Moat—the moat is a gap formed where the snow and ice are melted by the warmer rock along the edge of a glacier. The edge of a moat is often undercut. Depending on its size, the moat may be an obstacle to moving on or off the glacier. • Icefalls—icefalls result from the flow of the glacier down a steep ridge. The ridge forces the ice up into a jumbled mass as the glacier flows over the rock. These present formidable

to moving on or off the glacier. • Icefalls—icefalls result from the flow of the glacier down a steep ridge. The ridge forces the ice up into a jumbled mass as the glacier flows over the rock. These present formidable obstacles and should be avoided. • Serac—seracs are ice walls and towers that form in icefalls or on the lower edge of hanging glaciers. They are unstable and can fall unexpectedly. Travel below seracs or hanging glaciers should be avoided when possible. • Nunatak—a nunatak is an island of bedrock that protrudes up through the glacier, creating an obstacle to glacial movement. It creates pressure in the ice that can form crevasses, seracs, and icefalls. • Water hazards—streams that run on the surface and then disappear into a hole are called moulins. Moulins form when meltwater from the glacier finds a crevasse and moves to the ground below the ice. A fall into a moulin can carry a Soldier into the glacier and result in almost certain drowning. The glacial streams above this point must also be treated with respect. They are cold, can be deep, and the slick walls of their channels make them difficult to escape. In the

This water can freeze at night, forming glacial swamps. • Steep slopes—glaciers often include steep slopes that can create falling hazards, especially in firm snow conditions. • Moraines—moraines are piles of rock and other debris that have either fallen onto the glacier or been pried loose by it as it moves along. Glaciers are typically large open danger areas and should be treated as such during tactical operations. Units traveling on glaciers are subject to observation from all the surrounding high ground. A capable detachment may be required to provide an overwatch for the force traveling below. EQUIPMENT 14-9. Chapter 14 ICE AXE AND CRAMPONS 14-12. Ice axes and crampons may be necessary for movement over snow or ice on a glacier but also provide the ability for a Soldier on a rope team to self-arrest to control, stop, and hold the fall of another climber. Ice axes may also be used for snow anchor construction for crevasse rescue. SKIS AND SNOWSHOES 14-13. In deep snow conditions, skis or snowshoes make movement more efficient. They also distribute weight over a greater area when crossing crevasses, which can reduce the likelihood of breaking through a hidden snow bridge. Snowshoes may be more practical than skis for roped glacier travel unless all members of a rope team are skilled skiers. PRUSIKS, SLINGS, AND CORDELETTES 14-14. Short prusik loops, slings, and cordelettes can be used for ascending a rope after a crevasse fall. They are used for belaying rope team members and creating anchors, load transfers, and hauling systems in crevasse rescue. Slings can be used to improvise a chest harness, if necessary, and can be useful to rig the rucksack for removal in the event of a fall. Each Soldier should carry a cordelette, a sling, and a short prusik. SNOW

They can be used to mark the location of known crevasses on frequently used routes or used in pairs forming an X to indicate danger. They can be used while setting up bivouac sites to mark the boundaries of safe areas. They are sometimes useful for whiteout navigation in heavily crevassed terrain. Wands can be made using 4-foot bamboo garden stakes with tape or flagging. OTHER GLACIAL GEAR 14-17. USE OF THE ROPE 14-18. A central question when considering travel over glaciers is whether to use a rope for fall protection. The hazard of hidden crevasses on a glacier varies considerably. In some circumstances, it may be preferable to travel unroped on crevassed glaciers; however, this is not typical. Deciding whether to rope together as a team depends upon the season, mode of travel, snow conditions, and the conditions of the glacier itself. 14-19. Traveling unroped is faster. It makes communication and dissemination of information easier; it can be done with untrained Soldiers. It eliminates the transition times required for tying in and preparing for roped travel. It also allows for movement in tactical formations and a better security posture. 14-20. HAZARD VERSUS CREVASSE HAZARD 14-21. In glaciated terrain, there can be both a risk of falling on steep ground as well as a risk of falling into crevasses. These risks are not managed in the same way. Crevasse hazard is best managed with good route finding and by keeping 8 to 10 meters of rope between Soldiers. Rope teams can usually stop crevasse falls because these occur on low-angled terrain without falling hazard. On flat terrain or soft snow, the arresting Soldiers are not typically at risk of sliding into the crevasse and are often able to stop the fall by slumping in the snow, rather than a full team self-arrest. 14-22. Falls on steep firm snow or an icy slope have almost no chance of being stopped by a rope team. Steep fall hazard is better managed by belaying Soldiers individually as described in chapter 10 or simul-climbing with protection placed for the team. It can be tempting to travel on steep slopes using crevasse fall protection techniques, but this is an illusion of safety. It should not have unnecessary slack or be taut. Excess slack will cause a Soldier to fall deeper into a crevasse, placing more force on other members of the team and increasing the difficulty of arresting the fall. The falling climber is more likely to hit something or become stuck or wedged. 14-34. A rope with the correct amount of tension lies on the snow with a gentle curve, out of the way of the feet. It can be helpful to hold the rope to the front when traveling downhill and to the rear when traveling uphill. Pace should be adjusted to maintain correct tension in the rope by feel, especially during stops and starts. The Soldier in the lead should set a pace that others can easily follow. 340 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

During sharp turns, the rope tends to go slack as the lead Soldier makes a change in the direction of travel, but then it becomes taut as the next Soldier approaches the turn. Chapter 14 ROUTE FINDING AND CREVASSE DETECTIONS 14-37. Crevasse falls are extremely dangerous, even when traveling roped up with experienced Soldiers. Even when all Soldiers manage the rope well and the fall is stopped immediately, severe injuries can result. Ice axes, crampons, and collapsing snow bridges can cause injuries. Detection and avoidance are the primary skills needed to eliminate the need for crevasse rescue. On heavily crevassed glaciers, it is advisable to use an advanced party to scout and mark the safest route in advance of the main body. This can save hours of wandering, slow progress, and running into dead ends. Once relatively safe routes are established, it can reduce the skill and experience level required of the main body. INFORMATION GATHERING 14-38. Big picture views of the terrain can be very helpful. A maze of crevasses can be analyzed more easily from above than from within. It is a good idea to take digital photos whenever high ground provides a vantage point. Because glaciers move so slowly, crevasse patterns remain constant from year to year, making even old photographs useful for study. Intelligence products or online mapping resources (see appendix B) that contain satellite imagery can provide overhead

provides a vantage point. Because glaciers move so slowly, crevasse patterns remain constant from year to year, making even old photographs useful for study. Intelligence products or online mapping resources (see appendix B) that contain satellite imagery can provide overhead views. These may contain imagery taken during the summer or late season and show the general trends and locations of dense crevasses that may be only partially filled in or have suspect snow bridges when traveling during winter and early season. TIMING 14-39. On snow covered and heavily crevassed glaciers, snow bridges are firmer at night or early in the morning. If stable, they can often provide more direct lines of travel. Warmer daytime temperatures can soften these snow bridges, increasing the likelihood of crevasse fall. This may require finding a longer alternative route. 14-40. Be cautious after snowstorms. Fresh snow can fill in and blend in what might otherwise be detectable crevasses. 14-41. Seasonal timing is equally important. Although unit leaders may not have much say in the time of year they are required to travel on glaciers, a basic understanding of how seasonal changes affect surface conditions is important. Below are descriptions of typical conditions in the midlatitudes:

unit leaders may not have much say in the time of year they are required to travel on glaciers, a basic understanding of how seasonal changes affect surface conditions is important. Below are descriptions of typical conditions in the midlatitudes: • Autumn—in late season conditions, most crevasses are clearly visible and snow bridges have melted out to their maximum extent. Travel is generally safest, as there is little risk of unexpected crevasse fall, but route finding can be difficult and require long detours and lengthy movement times around crevasse fields. In steeper terrain, firm conditions can make falling hazard a higher concern. • Winter—early winter is especially hazardous. Unconsolidated snow hides crevasses but often does not effectively bridge them. Crevasses are more difficult to detect, and unexpected falls are more likely. In late winter, deeper snow conditions may provide more effective snow bridges. Increased snow loads may cause bridges to sag, making detection easier. Skis or snowshoes are often required. • Spring—snowfall has reached its maximum depth, making glacier travel safest. Snow bridges are at their strongest and the snowpack strengthens from warmer weather. Skis or snowshoes are often required, but lines of travel are typically much more direct. •

• Spring—snowfall has reached its maximum depth, making glacier travel safest. Snow bridges are at their strongest and the snowpack strengthens from warmer weather. Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue ZONES OF TENSION AND COMPRESSION 14-43. Crevasses are formed by tension. Tension is created as glacier ice stretches over rolls in the terrain and where it stretches due to different rates of flow within the glacier. These crevasses form perpendicular to the direction of the stretch. Recognizing where this tension is likely to occur can help with predicting their likely locations when snow fills in or conceals them. Crevasses are more likely at the top of a roll, where the terrain gets steeper and drops away below it. They are also common near the edges of valley glaciers, where additional drag and friction occurs against the valley walls, and the center of the glacier is moving faster. These “marginal” crevasses point toward the center of the glacier at an angle. For this same reason, the centers of glaciers generally have fewer crevasses and are preferred travel routes. 14-44. Compression zones occur where the underlying bedrock flattens out and where glacial ice slows down or piles up. Here, crevasses become narrow and eventually disappear. Glacial ice can also pile up in bowls and flat benches in the terrain and where glaciers flow together. These areas of

flattens out and where glacial ice slows down or piles up. Here, crevasses become narrow and eventually disappear. Glacial ice can also pile up in bowls and flat benches in the terrain and where glaciers flow together. These areas of compression can be relatively crevasse-free. Observing these zones and working to link them together are keys to good route finding. SURFACE CLUES 14-45. Clues to locating crevasses below the surface of the snow can be subtle and difficult to recognize, but it is important for determining an appropriate crossing technique. It can also be just as important to recognize similar clues that do not indicate crevasses and to not waste time and effort on long detours. • Sagging—snow covering larger crevasses gradually deforms and sags under its own weight. Early in the process, this may be barely noticeable, but later the outlines of the crevasse become more defined. Sometimes a slight change in sheen or texture can be observed. Other times, a slight change in color, from dust or windblown snow settling in a subtle depression, can be visible. These should be approached with caution. Snow is, however, an inherently uneven surface, so not every dip, groove, or color change

times, a slight change in color, from dust or windblown snow settling in a subtle depression, can be visible. These should be approached with caution. Snow is, however, an inherently uneven surface, so not every dip, groove, or color change represents a crevasse. In low visibility or flat light, these can be impossible to recognize. • Nearby crevasses—since crevasses are often found in groups and tend to form parallel to one another, look for other crevasses, patterns, or depressions nearby that have similar orientation. • Parallel cracks—in the case of larger crevasses, parallel thin cracks can sometimes form at the edges of a giant snow bridge. Although these can have the appearance of two narrow crevasses, they can be the boundaries of a single, giant snow bridge. PROBING 14-46. Snow probing in areas that look suspicious can be done using an ice axe. It can identify crevasses, determine its true lip, and investigate the extent, length, and width of a crevasse. To probe, the shaft of the axe is thrust into the snow a couple feet ahead of where one moves, looking for a noticeable reduction in resistance. If there is a sudden drop in resistance, there is likely a

crevasse. To probe, the shaft of the axe is thrust into the snow a couple feet ahead of where one moves, looking for a noticeable reduction in resistance. If there is a sudden drop in resistance, there is likely a crevasse, but it can also be a soft snow layer. Probing requires experience to accurately interpret. The short length of an ice axe makes this difficult. Avalanche probes and ski poles with the basket removed are better choices, if available. Probing is also required for determining safe bivouac locations. CROSSING TECHNIQUES 14-47. There are a variety of options and techniques for crossing crevasses, and leaders must understand and be capable of incorporating any combination of them to adapt to the terrain. Rope teams should travel perpendicular to the direction of crevasses to reduce the risk of exposing more than one Soldier at a time. (See figure 14-6, page 344.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 343

Sometimes it is preferable to cross at one end of a crevasse where its width narrows, rather than take a chance with a snow bridge. (See figure 14-7.) With large crevasses, this could lead to traveling a quarter of a mile or more to gain 30 feet of forward progress. In winter or spring, seasonal snow may still cover the narrow ends of a crevasse. What looks like the end of the crevasse might not be its actual end. This assessment can require some judgement. Make a wide swing, probe carefully, and cross at a right angle to the crevasse. 344 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

The remaining Soldier in the team provides a moving belay by controlling the slack and remaining ready to self-arrest. Once the leader is across, the rest of the team must follow exactly in the leader’s footsteps. At this point, the leader controls slack and remains prepared for self-arrest. Chapter 14 Jumping 14-50. Only conduct jumping when the gap is short. Running leaps requiring big push offs from suspect crevasse lips and falls can result in serious injury. Jumping should not be attempted unless there are no other options. Enough slack must be provided for the jumper to clear the crevasse without question. Be wary of catching a crampon and use common sense. Climbing into the Crevasse 14-51. Occasionally, it may be practical to climb down into a shallow crevasse and climb back out the other side. Standard belay techniques (see chapter 10) should be used. Be especially aware of bottoms that appear solid but are not. Echelon Formation 14-52. When it is impractical to travel perpendicular to existing crevasses and Soldiers must travel parallel, the echelon formation can be used. (See figure 14-9.) This keeps team members still to the rear but offset slightly to the side. This provides an alternative to following the leader’s tracks in a single-file line. This should only be used on heavily crevassed sections where all crevasses are visible and there is very little risk of falling into a hidden one. Figure 14-9. Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue CREVASSE FALL CONSIDERATIONS 14-54. Mutually supporting rope teams should have a minimum of one Soldier per team who is trained in crevasse rescue. This will ensure that rescue capability can always be provided, even when the more experienced member of another rope team is the one to fall in. Two trained Soldiers are necessary in rope teams traveling independently, away from supporting teams. 14-55. Crevasse falls are rarely dramatic and sudden falls that rip team members off their feet and result in someone dangling down inside an abyss. In fact, most crevasse falls involve breaking through a snow bridge but falling no further than waste deep, and with minimal force exerted on team members. Despite this, Soldiers must be trained to deal with more severe falls and be able to adapt and adjust to a variety of circumstances. Options for crevasse rescue involve an abundance of variables. They depend largely upon the breakdown of rope teams, the number of Soldiers per rope, conditions of the glacier, and specific equipment carried. A comprehensive and detailed description of crevasse rescue techniques is well beyond the scope of this publication. Instead, the steps and decision process typically used

A comprehensive and detailed description of crevasse rescue techniques is well beyond the scope of this publication. Instead, the steps and decision process typically used for a three-person rope team are described below. STEPS TO TAKE FOR CREVASSE FALL 14-56. The following steps should be considered in the event of a crevasse fall with a three-person rope team. STOP THE FALL 14-57. Stop the fall immediately. Some falls may be barely noticeable, while others may require dropping into the self-arrest position in the opposite direction. Stopping falls on firm surfaces can be more difficult than soft ones. Once the fall is arrested, both rescuers should kick crampon points into the snow to establish a strong, stable position to prevent the victim from slipping any further. Communication can often be made with the victim at this point. In circumstances where Soldiers have only fallen a few feet or are stuck in the snow bridge, they may be able to climb out unassisted. If a Soldier is not able to quickly self-recover, then the following steps must be taken. (See figure 14-10, page 348.) 26 November 2025

Chapter 14 Figure 14-10. Stopping a crevasse fall CONSTRUCT AN ANCHOR AND TRANSFER THE LOAD 14-58. When another rope team is available, then they can construct an anchor and help the team transfer the load of the fallen Soldier onto it. (See figure 14-11.) Otherwise, the Soldier on the opposite end is usually the one to complete this step. End Soldiers slowly get out of the self-arrest, making sure that middle Soldiers can still hold the weight. End Soldiers establish an anchor (see chapter 9 for snow and ice anchors) below the middle climber and towards the crevasse. They attach a prusik to the loaded rope and clip it to the anchor with a locking carabiner. If there is limited distance between the middle climber and the crevasse lip, the anchor can be constructed above the middle climber. In this case, the slack rope itself, between the middle and end climber can be used to attach directly to the anchor. 348 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue 14-59. Next, the end Soldiers get back into the self-arrest position to back up middle Soldiers as they transfer the weight of fallen Soldiers onto this prusik. Once pressure is relieved from middle Soldiers, it is common for them to continue backing up this anchor while the end climber improves it or constructs additional components. This anchor must be unquestionably strong, as it may be used to haul the Soldier out. The prusik should also be backed up with a suitable knot clipped to the anchor. Figure 14-11. Construct the anchor and transfer the load COMMUNICATE WITH THE FALLEN CLIMBER AND MAKE A PLAN 14-60. To make a clear assessment and develop a plan, it is best to approach the edge of the crevasse where the fallen Soldier can be seen and heard. This can be done by one of the team members using a safety prusik attached to the unweighted portion of the rope. Exercise caution approaching the edge. Determination of what to do next will depend on how far down the climbers are, whether they sustained injuries, extent of any injuries, and characteristics of the terrain in and around the crevasse. The loaded

Exercise caution approaching the edge. Determination of what to do next will depend on how far down the climbers are, whether they sustained injuries, extent of any injuries, and characteristics of the terrain in and around the crevasse. The loaded rope can often become entrenched into the lip of the crevasse, complicating rescue options. This may be a good time to pad underneath the rope to prevent this from becoming worse with an ice axe shaft, foam pad, or rucksack slid underneath the rope as close to the edge as can be reached. This can take some work, and items used for padding should be anchored so that it cannot fall into the crevasse. Various options for rescue are described below. Self-Rescue 14-61. Self-rescue can be achieved by the fallen climber ascending the rope itself using a prusik ascent (see paragraphs 11-39 through 11-49, pages 282 through 284) or other techniques discussed in chapter 11 and is also shown in figure 14-10, page 348. When possible, this is often the easiest and fastest option. The prusik ascent prevents the fallen Soldier from becoming cold waiting for rescuers. Getting the weight of the rucksack off the body and onto the rope

figure 14-10, page 348. When possible, this is often the easiest and fastest option. The prusik ascent prevents the fallen Soldier from becoming cold waiting for rescuers. Getting the weight of the rucksack off the body and onto the rope is also particularly helpful for staying upright. Assistance from team members may be required to surmount the crevasse lip. The method does not work if the fallen Soldier sustained significant injuries. Belay 14-62. Belays may be a fast, easy option when crampons and ice axes can be used to climb out of the hole, especially if or when the rope is too entrenched in the crevasse lip to prusik out. The remaining free end of the rope can be passed down to the fallen climber to tie into the harness with, while a team member above creates a belay at the anchor. Chapter 14 Haul 14-63. If none of the above options are viable, a more complex solution of hauling the fallen climber out will be needed. HAULING 14-64. Hauling techniques used for MA described in chapter 12 may be used for hauling; however, there are circumstances specific to working with crevasses that must be considered. Direct Haul 14-65. This refers to hauling systems constructed on the fallen climber’s weighted strand of rope. A common example is the 3:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-4, page 307.) This is constructed by untying the backup knot behind the prusik and using this remaining rope to construct the system. A disadvantage to the direct haul is that it does not work if the rope is entrenched in the crevasse lip. This method is also impractical if there are knots tied in the weighted rope to help hold the crevasse fall. (See figure 14-12.) Figure 14-12. Direct haul using a 3:1 hauling system 350 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue Drop Loop 14-66. Drop loops refer to hauling systems that use a bight of rope sent down and attach to the fallen climber’s harness, independent of the climber’s weighted strand. (See figure 14-13.) An example is the 2:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-3, page 307.) This is often the preferred method because the crevasse lip can be padded prior to hauling and because the victim can often assist by pulling on the strand opposite the haul strand. Drop-loop hauls do require victims to clip the bight of rope into the harness, so in the case of an unconscious victim, this step may need to be done by first rappelling to them then re-ascending. Drop-loop systems can be performed using the remainder of the rope or by a separate rope team utilizing a different rope altogether. Progress must still be captured during the haul for safety. This may be done by pulling rope through the prusik on the original tensioned rope. Figure 14-13. Drop-loop rescue system (2:1) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 351

Chapter 14 SECTION IV – TRAINING 14-67. Even when mutually supporting rope teams are used, good route finding, and crevasse detection skills are critical. Every rope team must have at least one Soldier with solid crevasse rescue skills. A lack of expertise can leave units with a large capability gap. 14-68. Training and experience in glacier travel are most productive when conducted on glaciers. Most glaciated terrain in the lower 48 states is in the Pacific Northwest. The high cost of travel and time commitments to access them make training plans difficult for units to execute. In the absence of glaciated terrain, units can still conduct simulated training exercises focusing on the basic strategies for roping up and preparing individual and team equipment. Chapter 15 Mountain Rescue and Evacuation A unit’s capability to conduct mountain rescue and evacuation is a critical part of mountain operations. Swift and efficient rescue can mean the difference between success and failure of a mission or even the survival of a casualty. In mountainous terrain, even relatively minor injuries may require evacuation. The type of injury, distance to be moved, terrain, training level of the team, and litter capabilities determine the evacuation technique chosen. Air evacuation is preferred. However, the weather, tactical situation, or operational ceiling of the aircraft may make this impossible. Therefore, it is imperative that all personnel are trained in mountain evacuation techniques and are self-sufficient. Casualties should be triaged before evacuation. The most experienced medical personnel available perform triage (physician, physician’s assistant, or medic). SECTION I – RESCUE OPERATIONS 15-1. Every commander should have a MEDEVAC plan before undertaking an operation. This plan should have dedicated assets (primary, alternate, contingency, and emergency) in place so as not to rely on a single evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes and gusting

so as not to rely on a single evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes and gusting winds reduce the ability of fixed-wing or rotary-wing aircraft to assist in operations. Therefore, relying solely on aircraft or specialized equipment is a poor substitute for careful planning. 15-2. The two types of rescue operations encountered by units operating in mountainous environments are deliberate and improvised. DELIBERATE 15-3. Deliberate rescue is when the mission objective itself is a rescue operation, thus allowing time for focused planning and the use of specialized rescue specific equipment. IMPROVISED 15-4. Improvised rescue situations are encountered when a casualty is sustained during normal operations and conducting a rescue was not the intended objective. Even improvised rescue operations should be practiced and rehearsed to minimize the negative effects on mission capability. All operations should have a CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. These plans must be understood by all who may be involved in a

CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. These plans must be understood by all who may be involved in a potential rescue. PLANNING 15-5. The rescue tasks must be identified by obtaining the following information: • Number of casualties by precedence (urgent, priority, routine, convenience). • Number of casualties by type (litter or ambulatory) and the nature of their injuries. • Terrain features and with respect to the location of the casualties. • Tactical situation. • Any assets available to aid in security, rescue, treatment, and evacuation. • If treatment can be provided at the scene or if the casualty requires movement to a safer location. • Additional personnel or equipment required for the rescue operation. • Any circumstances that may require specialized skills. • Weather conditions. • Difficulty of the terrain. • Time available. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 353

In some cases, trained personnel and equipment available for low- or high-angle rescue may allow for safer, less physically demanding operations. A lack of these resources and capabilities may require traveling longer distances around steeper terrain, greatly increasing the burden on rescuers. CONSIDERATIONS 15-7. Time considerations can cause a leader to compromise planning stages or treatment (beyond first aid). Make a realistic estimate of time available as quickly as possible to determine the action time remaining. The key elements are the casualty’s condition and ability to endure the environment. Time available is a balance between these conditions and the resources and personnel available. 15-8. Maximum use of secure, reliable trails or roads is essential. • Protection

extensive preparation and can involve establishing anchor points, belays, fixed ropes, lowers, and raises. • Altitude and visibility can greatly affect the team as well as the casualty. Maximum use of secure, reliable trails or roads is essential. • Protection from the elements, such as blankets, tarps, warming layers and rain gear, can be vital. Even a mild rain can complicate an otherwise simple rescue. In higher altitudes, extreme cold or strong winds can greatly increase the rescue’s time and complexity. GENERAL STEPS 15-9. Regardless of whether a rescue is deliberate or improvised, the following steps must be taken upon arrival at the rescue site to accomplish a safe and efficient rescue operation: • Assume command—one person and one person only is in charge. • Scene safety—prevent further injuries to the casualty and to others. Explore all options for casualty access prior to committing to one. Use reasonable care in reaching the casualty. Rescuers must not become casualties. • Immediately ensure the casualty has an open airway, control serious bleeding, and protect the casualty from further harm and from environmental hazards. If the casualty is unconscious, continually monitor for a pulse. • Do not move the casualty until determining the

ensure the casualty has an open airway, control serious bleeding, and protect the casualty from further harm and from environmental hazards. If the casualty is unconscious, continually monitor for a pulse. • Do not move the casualty until determining the extent of injuries unless necessary to prevent further injury or if the casualty is in a dangerous or exposed location. • Do nothing more until the situation has been thoroughly considered. evacuation route is long and arduous, a series of litter relay points or stations should be established, if possible. These help to manage the welfare of both the casualty and the rescue team. These stations should be staffed with the medical personnel and equipment necessary to provide proper treatment. • Helicopters or heated vehicles, if available, should be used for evacuation. PROLONGED FIELD CARE 15-11. The mountain environment is defined by austere and remote conditions. This environment, combined with the difficulty of patient movement, creates situations that can extend patient management over many hours or days. Prolonged field care is the continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care (JP 4-02). 15-12. Medical personnel with standard training

can extend patient management over many hours or days. Prolonged field care is the continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care (JP 4-02). 15-12. Medical personnel with standard training may be required to perform beyond their skillset. Specific training should be conducted to prepare medical and nonmedical personnel for prolonged field care situations. Tactical combat casualty care uses protocols aimed primarily at preventing mortality in the first few hours of treatment, prior to arrival at surgical resuscitative care. However, patients in the mountains lacking fast and immediate evacuation are often at risk for complications, such as sepsis, multi-organ system failure, respiratory compromise, and other serious conditions. Prolonged field care begins with the sound principles of tactical combat casualty care, but when care is extended over hours or days, treatment must continuously be re-evaluated. Diligence is necessary to minimize the effect of potentially harmful interventions and to prevent, recognize, and treat conditions that may develop over time. 15-13. Critical patients ultimately require care in a hospital with surgery, blood products, an intensive care unit, and advanced imaging. Casualties in the mountains can be moved and transported in a variety of ways, from simple manual field carries to high-angle evacuations using litters and complex rope systems. The type of injury, distance to be moved, time available, and resources will determine the best technique for a given situation. MOVING CASUALTIES WITHOUT LITTERS 15-15. There are varieties of circumstances where casualties may move, be moved, or be carried without the use of litters. This could be a result of sustaining relatively minor injuries, not having a litter available, or not having the available personnel for litter transport. Alternatively, these could involve moving a casualty in technical terrain that is not suited for transport in a litter. If casualties are able, they can walk, with one or more rescuers walking alongside, to provide physical support. A rescuer close behind can help in difficult terrain. not suited for transport in a litter. If casualties are able, they can walk, with one or more rescuers walking alongside, to provide physical support. In situations where the casualty cannot walk, simple techniques described in the Soldier’s Manual of Common Tasks (fireman’s carry, two-hand, four-hand, saddleback, piggyback, pistol belt, and poncho litter) may be useful. Casualties can also be placed in a seat or improvised harness and lowered or hauled through steep terrain using the techniques described in chapter 12. This may be done with ambulatory patients or may be necessary in situations where an injured Soldier must be moved from a cliff to an alternate location where packaging in a litter is more easily accomplished. This may require considerable assistance from rescuers or other Soldiers. It should only be attempted when necessary and after any immediate life-threatening injuries have been treated. Remember the more complex the technical rope systems become, the more time consuming they tend to be, increasing exposure and vulnerability to enemy attack. MOVING CASUALTIES IN LITTERS 15-21. Usually, casualties with significant injuries in the mountains need to be evacuated with the use of a litter. Several types of litters are available for transporting casualties in rough terrain. 358 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Rescue and Evacuation MANUFACTURED LITTERS 15-22. The following litters are readily available to mountaineering units: • The poleless, nonrigid litter is lightweight and readily available but is the least favored litter. It does little to protect the patient’s injuries and is not appropriate for attachment to any rope system. • The standard collapsible litter is readily available in all units and may be rigged for movement over rough mountainous terrain. However, it is not suitable for carry as a contingency litter due to its bulk and weight. • A rigid, metal-framed, basket-style litter that is rated for hoist operations is very well-suited for moving casualties through mountainous environments. These litters provide excellent patient protection and spinal immobilization, and when rigged properly, can readily attach to a variety of technical rope systems. The drawbacks to this type of litter are that it is heavy and is not designed to slide over surfaces. A single-wheel attachment is available, which vastly increases the efficiency of movement over moderate terrain but comes at the cost of an even greater weight to be carried. • The patient rescue and recovery collapsible litter system is a lightweight, semirigid, rollout plastic litter that can also be

the efficiency of movement over moderate terrain but comes at the cost of an even greater weight to be carried. • The patient rescue and recovery collapsible litter system is a lightweight, semirigid, rollout plastic litter that can also be rigged to meet rating requirements for hoist operations. The most commonly issued and used version in mountaineering is the rescue litter, which provides excellent patient support and protection. This is the preferred litter for mountain operations due to its versatility and relatively low weight. However, it is not a spinal immobilization device. A backboard must be used with this system for patients who have injuries to the shoulder area. This system will accommodate long and short backboards, scoop stretchers, and most other immobilization equipment. IMPROVISED LITTERS 15-23. Litters can be improvised in the field using several techniques, but all of them require construction materials and time, generally offer less patient protection, and are more prone to breakage. 15-24. Litters can be made by securing poles inside blankets, tarps, ponchos, jackets, shirts, sacks, or bags. Poles can be improvised from strong branches, tent supports, skis, and other similar items. 15-25. If poles cannot be found, a large item, such as a

Casualties must be packaged and secured to litters before movement in rough terrain. Proper packaging should achieve stabilization, immobilization, protection from hypothermia, and preparation for transport. Physically strapping a person into a litter is relatively easy but making it comfortable and effective can be a challenge. The needs of litter bound casualties are great and should not be overlooked or underestimated. The decisions made during initial packaging will affect the physical and mental outcomes for the casualty in the end. 15-27. Chapter 15 15-29. Consider protecting the insulating layers from casualties themselves if there is a possibility they could become incontinent. A trash bag or waterproof bag with leg holes cut in it can be filled with socks or T-shirts to form a diaper. Wrap the casualty as completely as possible, leaving only necessary areas exposed. When available, hot water bottles should be added and placed by the casualty’s axillary areas (armpits, groin) and the neck to provide active rewarming. MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES 15-30. ATP 4-02.13 covers general principles of handling and moving with litters—principles that apply in all terrain. However, in rugged mountainous terrain, teams must often move considerably slower. Extensive personnel may be required to ensure adequate rest and safety. Advanced teams may be useful for route selection and clearing. 15-31. For longer movements, it can be useful to add slings or cordelettes to the litter rim or handles for each litter bearer. These slings can be passed over the shoulders to the opposite hand, allowing each bearer to push down with the hand opposite the litter. This can help to reduce strain on the arm and hand carrying the litter, as well as providing some height adjustment. 15-32. In

This can help to reduce strain on the arm and hand carrying the litter, as well as providing some height adjustment. 15-32. In severely uneven terrain, such as talus or boulder fields, the pass-through technique can make movement safer for both the casualty and rescuers, provided extra personnel are available. To conduct the pass-through technique, simply have extra litter bearers take up static positions in the terrain ahead of the litter and as close to one another as possible. The litter is then passed forward into the hands of the extra litter bearers. As soon as litter bearers in the rear become obsolete, they move around and take up a new position further ahead in the direction of travel. They then wait until the litter reaches them and repeat the technique. This allows rescuers to remain still as the litter is transported, taking advantage of secure footing and stable positions. In this way, the litter is less likely to be dropped and litter bearers are less likely to sustain an injury attempting to move and carry the heavy load at the same time.

If a litter can be dragged, attaching ropes may make doing so easier and more controllable. Ropes can be attached to the front of the litter for dragging purposes as well as to the rear of the litter for use with a brakeman to slow the speed of the litter on gentle descents. Mountain Rescue and Evacuation LOW-ANGLE RESCUE 15-35. Low-angle rescue can generally be categorized by roped litter evacuations on low to moderately steep slopes where much of the weight of the casualty and rescuer is still supported by the ground. In this terrain, the litter slides along the slope, either up or down, depending on the direction of travel. The rope pathway should be cleared prior to casualty movement. All precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. In all situations, the rescue team should strive to solve the terrain problem safely with the least technical solution. ROPE ATTACHMENT 15-36. Rescue litters are generally oriented vertically during low-angle slope evacuations. (See figure 15-5.) The rescue rope is attached to a vertical attachment point at the head of the litter with a locking carabiner or carabiners. The rope is connected at the head of the litter for comfort and for ensuring that blood does not pool at the casualty’s head during transport. 15-37. Many techniques can be used to create a vertical attachment point at the head of the litter. (See figure 15-6, page 362.) Techniques may be improvised, based on the

In the case of the patient rescue and recovery system, use the short length of rope that comes with the system and follow the manufacturer’s instructions for creating this. 15-38. The end of the rescue rope can then be attached to this point with a figure eight on a bight and connected with a locking carabiner. In some situations, the rescue rope can be used to simply provide a tight belay for the casualty while litter teams carry a litter up or down slopes. Many of the various belay techniques described in chapter 10 are appropriate for this; however, the terrain must be gentle enough that there is no falling hazard to members of the litter team. ATTENDANTS 15-40. In steeper terrain where lowering or raising the litter from above is necessary, there is often a falling hazard for the litter team. If rescuers cannot safely walk beside the litter, it is typically advisable to use a single rescuer attached to the system as an attendant. This attendant’s primary responsibility is to ensure the litter and casualty do not roll over, become hung up on terrain obstacles, or create slack in the system. 15-41. One technique is to attach the rescue rope to the litter head using a bowline with a tail that is long enough to reach the bottom of the litter when stretched out. The litter and attendant can be lowered using various lowering techniques described in chapter 12. Select or construct extremely solid anchors, tie off the end of the rope to close the system, and apply appropriate hands-free backups. The rope pathway should be cleared prior to casualty movement, and all precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. A Soldier secured safely near the edge can often be helpful to relay commands and help control the speed of the lower. Avoid rope pathways with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential. 15-45. If it is necessary to lower the litter and attendant multiple rope lengths, multiple anchor stations and lowering teams may be required to achieve this. Complex situations such as this require excellent leadership, terrain assessment, and communication. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 363

Chapter 15 RAISING 15-46. The litter and attendant can be raised through steep terrain using the various hauling techniques described in chapter 12. This could be done by a hauling team from above using main force or by creating MA using one of the systems previously described. If using main force, a prusik or other friction hitch should be attached to the rope and anchored as a progress capture. An additional member on the haul team must be dedicated to managing the prusik during this method. If using MA, the hauling team must pull slow and steady and should be extremely aware of the loss of feel for the load. In either case, the rope pathway should be cleared prior to casualty movement, and all precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. A Soldier secured safely near the edge can often be helpful to relay commands and help control the speed of the haul. Avoid hauling in terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential. HIGH-ANGLE RESCUE 15-47. High-angle rescue generally refers to roped evacuations down steep cliffs and 5th-class terrain. High-angle rescue requires formal training, experience, excellent judgement, and good technical problem-solving skills. It often requires a substantial amount of time. Only level 2 and 3 military mountaineers should only conduct high-angle rescue, when necessary. There are often many variables involved in high-angle rescue, and thus, there is no prescriptive set way to deal with the many challenges that can be encountered. Because a combination of skills and techniques may ultimately be required, including climbing techniques, belays, rappels, hauling and lowering methods, or even the use of high lines, a comprehensive focus is well beyond the scope of this training circular. Rather, this section will focus on some of the fundamental principles and commonly used tools and techniques. LITTER RIGGING 15-48. Whether a rescue litter or a rigid metal basket is used for a high-angle evacuation, the rigging is similar. The litter can be rigged for horizontal orientation, like a helicopter hoist configuration, or it can be rigged for a vertical orientation the same as

or a rigid metal basket is used for a high-angle evacuation, the rigging is similar. The litter can be rigged for horizontal orientation, like a helicopter hoist configuration, or it can be rigged for a vertical orientation the same as described for lower-angle evacuations. In many cases, it is ideal to package the casualty in a manufactured or improvised harness. This allows the harness to connect to the rope system independently of the attachment to the litter itself. This can also be achieved with webbing using a variety of techniques. Horizontal Orientation 15-49. Horizontal orientation of the litter is often used in cases where the nature of the injury makes vertical orientation unsuitable, such as spinal, pelvic, and lower leg injuries. (See figure 15-8.) Severely hypothermic and cardiac patients should also be kept as horizontal as possible during transport. The rescue litter comes with two hoist straps that can be used for this. In the case of a similar metal basket litter, cordage or webbing can be rigged to connect the four corners to a single midline attachment point. (See figure 15-9.) Ensure the head end of the litter is slightly higher than the foot end, about 6 inches when

basket litter, cordage or webbing can be rigged to connect the four corners to a single midline attachment point. (See figure 15-9.) Ensure the head end of the litter is slightly higher than the foot end, about 6 inches when unloaded. Use locking carabiners and ensure that all carabiners used in the rigging are oriented correctly. It is easy to create a dangerous situation by cross-loading carabiners. 364 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Rescue and Evacuation Figure 15-8. Litter rigged horizontal orientation with hoist straps Figure 15-9. Basket litter rigged for horizontal orientation Vertical Orientation 15-50. Vertical litter orientation is often preferred as it can make for a simpler and more fluid edge transition. It is also lower profile, protects the patient better from rockfall and other hazards, and does not require a change in rope attachment point when transitioning to or from low-angle terrain. However, this method can be unsuitable for casualties with spinal, pelvic, and some lower leg injuries and requires securing the patient in such a way to minimize movement in the litter once evacuation begins. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 365

Chapter 15 ROPE SELECTION 15-51. Rope rescue systems should meet the industry standard 10:1 static system safety factor (SSSF). Calculate the SSSF by first determining the force created by the rescue load. Each person attached to the system is estimated to create 1 kN. Therefore, one casualty and one rescuer are estimated to be a 2-kN load. For a 2-kN load, all components of the rescue system must be rated to 20-kN breaking strength to meet the 10:1 SSSF requirement. In this case, ropes would require a minimum breaking strength of around 30 kN to account for an estimated 1/3 strength loss when knots are tied into the rope. Most static kernmantle ropes 11 mm in diameter meet this 30 kN threshold. However, for mountain rescue operations, it is much more practical to use lighter weight ropes that can more easily be carried, allow for faster response times, and function better with other components of the mountaineering kits. These may have MBSs that are a little less than 30 kN, but the advantages often outweigh the risks of encroaching on the very robust 10:1 SSSF. More important than the strength of a thinner diameter rope, users must be cognizant of

have MBSs that are a little less than 30 kN, but the advantages often outweigh the risks of encroaching on the very robust 10:1 SSSF. More important than the strength of a thinner diameter rope, users must be cognizant of edge abrasion issues. These ropes should be static (low stretch) and should have a minimum diameter of 9.5 mm and a minimum breaking strength of 26 kN. 15-52. Rescues can be carried out using single or tandem rope systems. Single Rope 15-53. Single rope technique, much like that described for use with low-angle rescue, is typically simpler to construct and operate, and generally requires less equipment overall. However, it does not include redundancy for system or rope failure. Equipment breakage or human error can have catastrophic results. Consider using this technique only when there is no prominent edge transition, no sharp rock edges on the pitch, and time and resources are limited. Tandem Rope 15-54. Tandem rope technique is more complex and time consuming, and gear intensive to construct. However, it has the added benefit of built-in redundancy against system or rope failure or human errors in rigging and operation. Consider tandem rope systems when there are prominent or difficult

complex and time consuming, and gear intensive to construct. However, it has the added benefit of built-in redundancy against system or rope failure or human errors in rigging and operation. Consider tandem rope systems when there are prominent or difficult edge transitions due to the potential for high-peak forces in the event of failure, sharp rock edges, or when there is limited team experience regarding the rigging of anchors and lowering or belay systems. 15-55. Tandem rope technique uses two separate ropes referred to as the main line and the belay line. Each rope system requires a separate anchor. The main line is used to haul or lower the litter, and the belay line is there in case of main line failure. 15-56. The two ropes are connected to the litter attachment point with interlocking long tailed bowlines. (See figure 15-10.) The tail or free end of each bowline is used as a secondary attachment point for the patient and the litter attendant. 366 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Chapter 15 Figure 15-11. Tandem prusik belay LOWERING 15-58. Sites suitable for lowering should have solid anchor points, good loading and unloading platforms, and good clearance for the casualty along the route. Terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential should be avoided when lowering is necessary. The litter and attendant can be lowered using various lowering techniques described in chapter 12, but techniques that generally provide greater friction are preferred. The end of the rope should be tied off to close the system. RAISING 15-59. Sites suitable for hauling should have solid anchor points, good loading and unloading platforms, and good clearance for the casualty along the route. Terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential should be avoided when hauling is necessary. The litter and attendant may be hauled using techniques described in chapter 12. Systems with higher ratios may be necessary, as well as redirection and piggyback techniques. BELAY LINE 15-60. While a properly constructed main line and solid anchor system should not fail, there is potential for a severe shock to the system if the attendant slips going over the edge. If such a slip occurs, the shock load will

While a properly constructed main line and solid anchor system should not fail, there is potential for a severe shock to the system if the attendant slips going over the edge. If such a slip occurs, the shock load will be significant due to the short amount of rope available to absorb the force, and the static nature of all the system components. The separate belay line is also here for this purpose. If a high directional is used, the belay line should not be routed through it. This would cause a greater fall distance before the belay line could catch the load in the event of failure or breakage of the high directional. 15-61. While there are manufactured devices available that meet the criteria for a technical rescue belay, the simplest and most field expedient method is called the tandem prusik belay. Two prusiks, preferably made from 7- or 8-mm nylon static utility cord are tied approximately 2-inches apart on the belay line. The length of the prusik closer to the anchor should be a few inches shorter than the other prusik. These prusiks are then attached to the belay anchor with a locking carabiner. To use the belay,

Precise commands and singular control are necessary for safe operations. All commands should originate either with the team leader, control, or, in some cases, the edge safety. A variety of commands can be used but must be short, simple, and clear. Always include the name of the position in the command, such as SLACK ON MAIN or TENSION ON BELAY. Before any lowering or raising operations take place, a roll call is necessary to ensure all personnel are ready. The roll call should start with personnel near or at the edge and work backwards to the main. Once all personnel are ready and checked and the litter and attendant are in position, begin the operation by calling UP ON MAIN or DOWN ON MAIN. Once the litter is moving, the speed can be adjusted, as necessary. To halt all movement, call STOP. All teams continue to act as if the load is on belay until the command OFF BELAY is given. 15-71. Chapter 16 Rope Bridges Operations in mountainous terrain often encounter obstacles, such as fast flowing water, ravines, or rock fields. Well-trained mountaineers can exploit this terrain with the use of rope bridges and high lines. These allow units to take the terrain out of the equation by using a rope suspended in the air to cross the obstacle. High lines are a type of rope bridge. The two terms are often used synonymously, and the techniques are relatively interchangeable; however, for the purposes of this training circular, we will refer to rope bridges when used for assisting personnel for river crossings and the term “high lines” to denote rope installations used to span longer or higher gaps in terrain. SECTION I – TECHNIQUES 16-1. A rope bridge is a rope tensioned between two anchors and suspended off the ground to assist units with crossing rivers. These are sometimes necessary in situations with swift and dangerous currents or very cold water, where keeping the majority of Soldiers dry is important. 16-2. Rope bridges can pose distinct disadvantages. Though linear in nature, rope bridge crossings in a tactical environment should be considered VDAs. This is because units establishing and using them are

where keeping the majority of Soldiers dry is important. 16-2. Rope bridges can pose distinct disadvantages. Though linear in nature, rope bridge crossings in a tactical environment should be considered VDAs. This is because units establishing and using them are fixed and potentially split by the river obstacle for prolonged periods. This can put them at a significant tactical disadvantage. (See ATP 3-21.50 for more VDA-crossing considerations.) CONSTRUCTION 16-3. The rope bridge is constructed using a static rope. The rope is anchored on the far side of the obstacle in the same manner as described for using handlines in paragraphs 13-26 through 13-29, page 327. It is then tensioned and anchored on the near side of the obstacle. A rope bridge may be built many ways depending upon the tactical situation and area to be crossed. However, all rope bridges share common safety principles for construction and use. Rope bridges must be tensioned as low as practical on the anchor while still facilitating suspending loads and off-loading them. The creation of artificial height (covered later) can be used for rope bridges. The type and location of the tensioning system depend on terrain and situation. METHODS OF TENSIONING 16-4. There are

while still facilitating suspending loads and off-loading them. The creation of artificial height (covered later) can be used for rope bridges. The type and location of the tensioning system depend on terrain and situation. METHODS OF TENSIONING 16-4. There are multiple ways to apply tension to a rope. The method selected depends on the length of the bridge, equipment available, personnel available, and time. Regardless of the method used, the principle remains the same; apply just enough tension to facilitate ease of crossing through the terrain. WARNING Ropes must not be overtensioned. An overtensioned rope is in its weakest state, and the system can apply exponential forces during use. Critical failures can occur with overtensioned ropes. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 371

Chapter 16 HAND TIGHT 16-5. The simplest and least equipment-intensive method is hand tightening the rope. Once Soldiers anchor one side of the rope, they pull the rope as tight as they can. Next, they tie off the rope using one of three methods: mule knot secured with an overhand knot (see figure 16-1), round turn around anchor and two half hitches on a bight, or a high strength tie off (tensionless hitch). A rope bridge constructed with a single rope has the risk of critical failure due to cutting and lacks redundancy. A redundancy (in rigging) is the condition in which a rope system will not fail as the result of any single component of the system failing. If the risk or critical nature of the load requires an additional level of redundancy, a second rope bridge may be constructed parallel to the first one. Examples of critical loads are a casualty, Soldiers crossing a rope bridge

failing. If the risk or critical nature of the load requires an additional level of redundancy, a second rope bridge may be constructed parallel to the first one. Examples of critical loads are a casualty, Soldiers crossing a rope bridge that is high off the ground, and a dry river crossing where a separate belay rope is not used. If two ropes are used, they should be as close as possible so that a single carabiner can be clipped to both lines. An individual would attach to both ropes when crossing, thus having a backup in case of failure. Redundancy is not always necessary or practical but is typically used in training as a risk management tool. METHODS OF CROSSING 16-14. A high line is a type of suspended rope bridge used to transport equipment or casualties high above difficult terrain that might otherwise be impassable. These can be used for personnel movement as well, although this is less common. The high line is used over large rivers, ravines, chasms, or diagonally from the top of a cliff to the ground below. The system may be established on different planes, varying from horizontal to near vertical. High lines keep the load suspended above the terrain as it travels directly between the nearand far-side anchors. 16-34. High lines come with a high level of risk due to the height of the load above the ground. High lines used for personnel movement require careful calculation to ensure system failure will not occur, resulting in catastrophic fall injury. They should only be constructed by advanced or master military mountaineers who have been formally trained in high-line construction for this purpose. SITE SELECTION

Appendix A Climbing Route Classification The most important tools for risk management in the mountains are route selection and evaluation. Accurately evaluating and selecting routes in high consequence terrain requires a well-developed understanding of technical route classification systems and experience climbing the terrain they describe. Route classifications allow military mountaineers to identify appropriate routes for their Soldiers’ skill levels and the technical rope systems required to move on them safely. Misunderstanding or miscommunicating route difficulty can place the life of the mountaineer or the lives of the Soldiers they lead in danger. The U.S. military does not have its own technical route classification systems. Therefore, military mountaineers must use those developed for civilian mountaineering. The classifications discussed in this chapter breakdown and describe the difficulty associated with routes in various types of terrain. Understanding them provides military mountaineers with the base from which to build route identification and selection experience. ROCK CLIMBING CLASSIFICATIONS A-1. There are several systems for classifying different aspects of rock-climbing difficulty. Different types of climbing require different classifications. Also, skill is not the only factor involved in classifying difficulty. The amount of time and effort necessary to complete a climbing route is often more important than

different aspects of rock-climbing difficulty. Different types of climbing require different classifications. Also, skill is not the only factor involved in classifying difficulty. The amount of time and effort necessary to complete a climbing route is often more important than what the hardest move on it is. Depending on the type of route being planned, one or all these route difficulty systems should be considered. YOSEMITE DECIMAL SYSTEM A-2. In North America, the YDS is used to rate the difficulty of rock-climbing routes. It categorizes terrain according to the techniques and physical difficulties encountered when rock climbing. The YDS classes are— • Class 1—hiking. • Class 2—off-trail scramble with the occasional use of hands. • Class 3—moderate scrambling, with short steps of easy climbing. Ropes may be used for beginners, but a guide can often manage the terrain with good coaching and modeling. • Class 4—simple climbing, with exposure. A rope is often used. A fall could be fatal. • Class 5—rock climbing. Usually requires climbers to rope up, belay, and place protection to protect the leader from a long fall. A-3. Class 5 is further subdivided to rate the difficulty of the climbing. The YDS only rates the hardest

Class 5—rock climbing. Usually requires climbers to rope up, belay, and place protection to protect the leader from a long fall. A-3. Class 5 is further subdivided to rate the difficulty of the climbing. The YDS only rates the hardest move on a pitch and does not account for strenuousness, difficulty of placing protection, or quality of the protection: • Class 5.0 to 5.4—easy. This is the simplest form of free climbing. Hands are necessary to support balance. Easy for experienced climbers. • Class 5.5 to 5.6—intermediate. Often no more physically difficult than easier climbing but requires trusting friction and smaller holds. The climber can experience vertical position or overhangs where there are positive holds that require moderate levels of energy expenditure. • Class 5.7 to 5.8—moderate. Considerable climbing experience is necessary. Longer stretches of climbing requiring several points of intermediate protection. Climbing often requires specific techniques, such as jamming, liebacks, or mantles. • Class 5.9 to 5.10—hard. Requires well above average ability and excellent condition. Exposed positions, often combined with small belay points. Passages of the difficult sections can often be accomplished under good conditions. Often combined with aid climbing. • Class 5.11 to 5.15—very difficult. Requires more climbing

above average ability and excellent condition. Exposed positions, often combined with small belay points. Passages of the difficult sections can often be accomplished under good conditions. Often combined with aid climbing. • Class 5.11 to 5.15—very difficult. Requires more climbing ability, experience, and energy expenditure. Only talented and dedicated climbers reach this level. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 385

It is rated not by the physical difficulty of the climbing but the quality and spacing of the placements for gear: • A0—French-free. No aiders are required.
